parallelCase.title: Tegan and Desmond on Karrow Isle
parallelCase.summary:
Setting: Karrow Isle, a fictional island. It has one primary school, a small health centre and a council that runs adult social care from the mainland.
Tegan Pascoe, age 7: She has severe hearing loss in both ears, found at age three. She wears hearing aids and is learning British Sign Language.
Tegan's support: She has an Education, Health and Care plan. A teacher of the deaf visits her school once a week.
Tegan's strengths: She signs with her friends and loves swimming. Her number work is typical, but her reading is behind her age group.
Tegan's family: Her mother has cut her working hours to attend appointments. The family travel to the mainland for audiology (hearing tests).
Desmond Carne, age 61: Two years ago he had a brain injury in a cycling accident. He has memory problems, tiredness and difficulty planning his day.
Desmond's life: He lives alone and cooks for himself. He uses a personal health budget to pay for a support worker three mornings a week.
Desmond's support: He goes to a weekly peer group run by a mainland charity. His daughter helps with bills.
What may change: The council is reviewing its adult social care budget, so his hours may be reduced.

requirements.need: Reach a judgement about how much the diagnosis matters for the individual, the family and society. Do not just describe each.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate long-term effects on the individual, family and society, reaching reasoned and valid judgements.
requirements.means: Evaluate means weighing up which effects matter most and for whom, then saying so. A description of effects on three groups is only the first step.
requirements.example: For Tegan, the diagnosis matters most to her own language and friendships. In the short term the family feels it hardest because of lost work hours and ferry trips. Society's share, mainly education and health costs, is smaller but lasts the longest.
requirements.nearMiss: Tegan's diagnosis affects her language and friendships, her family through her mother's reduced hours and ferry trips to the mainland, and society through education and health costs. Each group faces different effects.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It covers all three groups with accurate detail. But it gives them equal weight. It never says which matters most or why.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why does the example rank the effects instead of just listing them? What would be lost if it simply said 'it affects everyone'?

check.q: Which sentence makes a judgement about how much Tegan's diagnosis matters?
options: Tegan's diagnosis affects Tegan, her family and society, and each group has different needs.
Tegan's diagnosis led to hearing aids, a weekly teacher of the deaf and an EHC plan for her.
Tegan's diagnosis is significant, because severe hearing loss in both ears is a serious condition.
The family feels the diagnosis hardest in the short term, but society's costs last longest.
check.why: The key weighs the groups against each other and over time, which is a judgement. The tempting option covers all three groups but never says which matters most, which is the Merit-level trap of analysis without a verdict.

requirements.need: Cover emotional, physical, social, intellectual and financial impact. Do this for all three groups.
requirements.fromSpec: Consider emotional, physical, social, intellectual and financial impact on the individual, family and society.
requirements.means: Make sure none of the five types of impact is missing. Where one does not apply, say why in a few words.
requirements.example: Desmond's tiredness limits what he can do (physical), and forgetting appointments feeds his frustration (emotional). The cost to society is mainly financial, through his budget, while his daughter carries unpaid time as well as worry.
requirements.nearMiss: Desmond's tiredness limits what he can do (physical), forgetting appointments frustrates him (emotional) and planning his day is hard (intellectual). His support worker costs money (financial).
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names several types of impact for Desmond, correctly. But it never covers his daughter or society. So not all three groups are addressed.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which two types of impact does the example link? Why is linking them better than treating each one separately?

check.q: A learner's answer covers only the emotional and physical impact on Tegan. Which change best meets the guidance?
options: Explain the physical and emotional impact in more depth, since depth earns higher marks.
Cover social, intellectual and financial impact too, for Tegan, her family and society.
Cover all five types of impact for Tegan alone, since the guidance is about the individual.
Add Tegan's family and society, but keep to physical and emotional impact for each.
check.why: The guidance asks for all five types across all three groups, so both gaps must be filled. Going deeper on the same two types is the tempting move because depth feels like Distinction, but it leaves three types missing.

requirements.need: Back each conclusion with detailed analysis and research from recognised sources.
requirements.fromSpec: Use detailed analysis and research from recognised sources to reach valid, justified conclusions.
requirements.means: Say where your evidence comes from (for example a national charity or an NHS source). Use it to support your point. Do not add it just for show.
requirements.example: A national deaf children's charity reports that language delay is a common risk when hearing loss is found late. That supports the view that Tegan's reading gap is linked to her hearing loss, not to a lack of ability, because her number work is typical.
requirements.nearMiss: A national deaf children's charity reports that language delay is a common risk when hearing loss is found late. Tegan was diagnosed at three, and her reading is behind her age group.
requirements.whyNearMiss: A named source and Tegan's facts both appear, but they sit side by side. It never uses the research to argue that her reading gap comes from her hearing loss and not from ability.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example do with the source after quoting it? Say in your own words how that makes the conclusion stronger.

check.q: Which use of research is strongest when judging why Tegan's reading is behind?
options: Naming a deaf children's charity report, then using it to explain Tegan's reading gap.
Quoting several named reports on deafness one after another to show the range of reading.
Stating that national research shows deaf children often struggle with reading at school.
Copying a definition of severe hearing loss from a named health website, with no comment.
check.why: A named source only supports a conclusion when it is used to explain something specific, here Tegan's reading gap. Stacking named reports is the tempting option: it looks like thorough research but never applies any of it to the case.

requirements.need: Focus on long-term effects. Keep your arguments short.
requirements.fromSpec: Learners will articulate arguments and views concisely; evaluate possible long-term effects.
requirements.means: Look ahead to adulthood and later life as well as now. Keep each argument short and clear, with the judgement first.
requirements.example: Left unsupported, Desmond's difficulty planning could lead to loneliness within a few years, because he has few other contacts on the island. This makes the peer group the most important part of his long-term wellbeing.
requirements.nearMiss: Desmond's brain injury is likely to affect his memory and planning for many years. Living alone, he may find daily tasks hard and may feel lonely at times.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It points to a long period and to possible loneliness. But it never argues how lack of contact leads to later decline, or which long-term need matters most.
requirements.explainPrompt: Find the 'because' in the example. Why does that word matter for a long-term judgement?

check.q: Which sentence argues a long-term effect for Desmond, rather than just stating one?
options: His brain injury is likely to last, so Desmond will keep having memory problems for many years.
His support hours may be cut next year, which would make daily planning harder for him.
Without regular contact he may become isolated, which could worsen his memory and mood.
Desmond has memory problems, tiredness and trouble planning his day, and he lives alone.
check.why: A long-term effect needs a predicted later consequence and the reason for it. The most tempting wrong option says the injury will last, which states duration but argues no consequence.

requirements.need: Justify why each support or adaptation is right for the person. Use research.
requirements.fromSpec: Use research to justify the appropriateness of support and adaptations that help individuals overcome challenges.
requirements.means: Justify means giving reasons why it is the right choice for this person. Compare it with another option if you can.
requirements.example: A support worker is a sensible fit for Desmond because brain injury guidance stresses routine and prompts. Visits on three mornings give structure without taking away his independence, which an all-day carer would.
requirements.nearMiss: Three mornings of support suit Desmond because they help him plan his day. This is sensible because his memory problems make daily planning hard.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives a reason linked to Desmond. But it cites no research and compares no other option. So the choice is reasoned, but not justified at Distinction level.
requirements.explainPrompt: What is the example comparing the support worker with? Why does that comparison make it a justification?

check.q: Which sentence justifies the support worker for Desmond, not just describes it?
options: The support worker visits Desmond three mornings a week and helps with his daily tasks and planning.
Three mornings suit Desmond because brain injury guidance stresses routine, unlike an all-day carer.
A support worker is helpful for Desmond because it makes his week easier to manage day to day.
A personal health budget is the best way to pay for a support worker for people like Desmond, who live alone.
check.why: Justification gives a reason the support suits this person, backed by evidence and a comparison with alternatives. The tempting description is accurate and applied to Desmond, but it only says what the support is, which is the Merit-level trap.

requirements.need: Refer to the law that applies, and show what it gives each person.
requirements.fromSpec: Refer to relevant statutory guidance, e.g. EHC plans and local offers for children; personal health budgets for adults.
requirements.means: Name the law or system, say what it gives the person, and judge how well it works. Local authorities now run their own early help assessments, and some are still called CAF (Common Assessment Framework). Check which one your area uses.
requirements.example: Tegan's Education, Health and Care plan, set up under the Children and Families Act 2014, legally commits the school and health services to provide her teacher of the deaf. Without it her weekly support would depend on goodwill.
requirements.nearMiss: Tegan's Education, Health and Care plan was set up under the Children and Families Act 2014 and commits the school and health services to provide her teacher of the deaf.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names the Act and what the plan provides, correctly and for Tegan. But it does not judge why the plan matters, for example how it protects her support if budgets get tighter.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why does the phrase 'depend on goodwill' strengthen the example? Explain it as if to a classmate.

check.q: Which statement uses the law (statutory provision) at Distinction level for Tegan?
options: Tegan's EHC plan was set up under the Children and Families Act 2014 for children with special needs.
Tegan's EHC plan lists her teacher of the deaf and is reviewed by her school each year.
Her EHC plan gives Tegan a legal right to named support, which protects it if budgets tighten.
Statutory support is provided by law, and Tegan's plan is one example of statutory provision for her.
check.why: The key shows what the law gives Tegan and why it matters to her. Naming the Act is the tempting Merit-level option: it identifies the provision but never says what it gives her.

requirements.need: Apply what you know to a harder, less familiar situation.
requirements.fromSpec: Apply understanding to less familiar situations.
requirements.means: Go beyond the obvious case. For example, look at several supports at once, or a challenge that leads to another challenge.
requirements.example: Tegan's hearing loss limits her reading, which could reduce her confidence in class. Her support therefore needs to join up speech and language therapy with the teacher of the deaf, because treating each alone would miss that link.
requirements.nearMiss: Tegan's hearing loss limits her reading, and she has support from hearing aids and a teacher of the deaf. Her reading may also affect her confidence in class.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It notes the link between hearing, reading and confidence. But it stops there. It does not say what combined support those linked challenges need.
requirements.explainPrompt: What second challenge does the example find hiding behind the first? Why does that change what support is needed?

check.q: Which response applies what you know to Tegan's more complex situation?
options: Describing her hearing aids and her teacher of the deaf as two separate supports at school.
Adding that many deaf children use hearing aids and learn British Sign Language at school.
Defining severe hearing loss and stating the age at which Tegan's loss was found.
Explaining that her hearing loss limits her reading, so her supports must be joined up.
check.why: The key links one challenge to another and says what combined support follows. The tempting separate-supports option is accurate and applied to Tegan, but it treats each support alone and never shows how her challenges connect.

requirements.need: Weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of the support for both individuals.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate the advantages or otherwise of the support provided to the two individuals.
requirements.means: Evaluate means looking at gaps and drawbacks too. Do not only say the support is good.
requirements.example: The personal health budget gives Desmond control, but it only covers three mornings. In the afternoons, when his fatigue is worst, he has no support, so the benefit is real but incomplete.
requirements.nearMiss: The personal health budget gives Desmond control, and it pays for a support worker on three mornings. It does not cover the afternoons.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It states one advantage and one limit, correctly. But it never weighs them against each other. It does not say how much the gap matters to him.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which words in the example show that something is missing from Desmond's support?

check.q: A learner says the support 'works well' for both people. What is missing for Distinction?
options: Any limits or gaps, weighed against the benefits with evidence.
More detail on how each person's support is arranged and who provides it.
A third example of support for each person, to show wider coverage of help.
The same view restated more firmly, using stronger positive wording.
check.why: Evaluation weighs disadvantages as well as advantages, using evidence. Adding more detail about the support is the tempting fix, but it only lengthens the description.

requirements.need: Reach a justified conclusion about how well the support worked for wellbeing in one or more areas of development.
requirements.fromSpec: Reach justified conclusions about how effective support was for improving wellbeing in one or more areas.
requirements.means: Say how well it worked and in which areas (physical, intellectual, emotional, social). Use evidence such as an interview or an observation.
requirements.example: Tegan's signing group improved her social wellbeing, as her teacher reports she now plays with classmates. Her intellectual wellbeing has gained less, since her reading age is still behind, so the support is partly effective.
requirements.nearMiss: Tegan's signing group improved her social wellbeing, as her teacher reports she now plays with classmates. Her reading is still behind her age group.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Both areas have evidence. But the answer never says how effective the support is overall. The evidence is reported, not judged.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example decide that the support is only 'partly' effective? What evidence does it rely on?

check.q: Which is a justified conclusion about how effective Tegan's support has been?
options: Tegan's support has helped her wellbeing in several different ways, so it has been very effective.
It improved her social wellbeing, as she plays with classmates, but her reading is still behind.
Her social wellbeing has improved, which shows the support has been fully effective for her.
Her reading age is still behind, which shows the support has not been effective for her.
check.why: A justified conclusion names an area, gives evidence for it and says how far the support worked. The tempting 'fully effective' option has real evidence for one area but stretches it into a verdict on all of them.

requirements.need: Use research to judge the short-term and long-term effects of early intervention (help given early) on wellbeing and life chances.
requirements.fromSpec: Reach justified conclusions on possible long- and short-term effects of early intervention on wellbeing and life chances.
requirements.means: Compare what early support changes now with what it might change in adulthood, using research to back it up.
requirements.example: Tegan's support at three should help her language catch up before secondary school. Research from deaf charities suggests earlier support improves later education and work chances, so delay could have cost her more than the weekly visits cost the council.
requirements.nearMiss: Research from deaf charities suggests earlier support improves later education and work chances, and Tegan has had support since she was three.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It cites research and applies it to Tegan. But it never judges the effect, for example whether it will close her reading gap or how its benefit compares with its cost.
requirements.explainPrompt: What are the 'short-term' and 'long-term' effects in the example? Where is the research used?

check.q: Which sentence best uses research to judge the long-term effect of early support on Tegan?
options: Research links earlier language support to better school and work outcomes, so Tegan's help matters.
Early support helped Tegan make friends at school this year, which shows how well it works.
Deaf charities' research shows that deaf children benefit from early support, and Tegan has had some.
Early support costs the council a weekly visit, so it is an expense that the council can review later.
check.why: Life chances are later opportunities such as qualifications and work, and the key links early help to them through research. The research-name option is tempting because it cites evidence, but it never says what that means for Tegan's later chances.

requirements.need: Justify any recommendations using research, so that they are valid.
requirements.fromSpec: Refer to relevant research to justify the validity of recommendations and proposals.
requirements.means: If you suggest better support, explain why it would work. Use evidence such as research or professional interviews.
requirements.example: The council should keep Desmond's peer group funding, as brain injury charities report that peer contact reduces isolation. It is cheaper than crisis care and protects his independence.
requirements.nearMiss: The council should keep Desmond's peer group funding because it protects his independence and is cheaper than crisis care.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives reasons linked to Desmond. But it cites no research or professional source. So the recommendation is argued, but not backed up.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why is the example's recommendation more convincing than the near miss?

check.q: Which recommendation about Desmond is valid at Distinction level?
options: Increase Desmond's support hours, because he has a brain injury and lives alone on the island.
Keep the peer group funded, because it is cheaper than the crisis care he might otherwise need.
Keep the peer group funded, because the council already pays for it and he attends every week.
Keep the peer group, because brain injury charities report that contact cuts isolation.
check.why: A valid recommendation is backed by research or professional evidence and tied to the person's needs. The cost option is tempting because it sounds like reasoning, but it is an assertion with no evidence behind it.

parallelCase.title: Tarn Valley Cottage Hospital Laboratory
parallelCase.summary:
Setting: Tarn Valley Cottage Hospital, a fictional small hospital. Its pathology laboratory serves two care homes.
This week: The lab receives a urine sample from a care home resident with a suspected urinary tract infection. The sample is labelled but not yet identified.
Hospital lab steps: The sample is handled in a safety cabinet and logged on the lab's record system. It is cultured on agar plates.
Another request: A ward patient needs a pulse oximeter reading. This is an in vivo test (done in the living body).
Student mock lab: College students swab a tap in their building and grow the bacteria on nutrient agar. They Gram stain the colonies and view them under two magnifications.
Student disinfectant test: They also make a serial dilution of a disinfectant to see which strength stops growth.
Problems: One plate is contaminated. One stain fades within a day.
The task: Compare the students' methods with the hospital lab. Decide how useful each technique is for helping a doctor reach a diagnosis.

requirements.need: Justify each lab procedure by giving the reason it is used in this laboratory.
requirements.fromSpec: Use detailed analysis and research to justify procedures, relating them to the laboratory context.
requirements.means: Do not just say what happens. Say why it happens in this type of lab, with evidence.
requirements.example: In Tarn Valley's lab, the unidentified urine sample is opened in a safety cabinet because the organism might be harmful to staff. This justifies the extra time, since an infection in a care home could spread.
requirements.nearMiss: The unidentified urine sample is opened in a safety cabinet, which is standard practice in the lab, before it is cultured on agar plates.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is accurate and set in the lab. But 'standard practice' says what is done, not why. It never explains the risk from an unidentified organism.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which words in the example give a reason? Why does it matter that the reason relates to the care home?

check.q: Which sentence justifies a procedure used in the Tarn Valley lab?
options: The urine sample is opened in a safety cabinet and then spread onto agar plates for culture.
The urine sample is opened in a safety cabinet, which is the standard way to handle it here.
The urine sample is opened in a safety cabinet because unknown organisms could harm staff.
The urine sample is opened in a safety cabinet, as the lab's own written procedures require.
check.why: A justification gives the reason for a step, here the risk from an unidentified organism. The 'standard way' option sounds like a reason, but saying a step is routine or required explains nothing about why it is done.

requirements.need: Include health and safety measures and ways of recording. Justify both.
requirements.fromSpec: Procedures must include health and safety and recording methods.
requirements.means: Cover safety (such as COSHH rules for hazardous substances, PPE such as gloves, and safe disposal) and how samples are labelled and recorded. Say why each is needed.
requirements.example: Labelling the sample before it leaves the care home reduces the risk of a wrong result being given to the wrong resident. Logging each step on the record system lets staff trace a mistake, so it protects both patients and staff.
requirements.nearMiss: All samples are labelled and logged on the record system, and staff wear gloves and use the safety cabinet. This keeps patients and staff safe.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It covers both safety and recording. But it only says they keep people safe. It justifies neither, for example how labelling stops a result going to the wrong resident.
requirements.explainPrompt: What harm could happen if the labelling step failed? How does the example show that?

check.q: A learner explains PPE and waste disposal but not recording. What should be added?
options: Why gloves and lab coats are worn, such as to protect the skin from splashes.
Which disinfectant is used on the benches, with its strength and contact time.
How the final result is reported to the doctor, such as by phone or on the system.
Why samples are labelled and logged, such as to trace a result to the patient.
check.why: Recording methods such as labelling and logging are a separate requirement from health and safety, and must also be justified. Extra safety detail is the tempting error, as it deepens one half while the recording half stays missing.

requirements.need: Support conclusions with research from named sources and state them professionally.
requirements.fromSpec: Learners must articulate arguments concisely and professionally, and use research to justify conclusions.
requirements.means: Use reliable guidance (for example from the Health and Safety Executive or the UK Health Security Agency). Write in a formal, short style.
requirements.example: Health and Safety Executive guidance expects staff to assess the risk before handling any biological agent. This supports the lab's practice of treating all unidentified samples as potentially hazardous.
requirements.nearMiss: The Health and Safety Executive publishes guidance on handling biological agents, and the Tarn Valley lab follows safe handling procedures.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names a proper source and the lab. But the guidance is not used to support any practice. The source is mentioned, not used.
requirements.explainPrompt: Rewrite the near-miss sentence in your head: what source and wording would make it professional? Say what you would change.

check.q: Which sentence uses research in the most professional way?
options: A health website says labs must be careful with samples, so the lab's caution is right.
Guidance from the Health and Safety Executive is long and covers many laws and rules for labs.
Health and Safety Executive guidance requires risk assessment, which supports the lab's caution.
It is well known that biological samples are risky, which supports the lab's caution in handling.
check.why: Professional use names the source and uses its content to support a specific lab practice. Naming a body without using its content, the tempting option, shows a source exists but supports no conclusion.

requirements.need: Justify why you chose each technique for the outcome you wanted.
requirements.fromSpec: Justify decisions in using chosen techniques and methods in terms of results and the desired outcome.
requirements.means: State the outcome first (for example, find the shape and Gram type of the bacteria). Then say why the technique fits it.
requirements.example: The aim was to tell whether the tap bacteria were Gram positive or negative. A Gram stain was chosen because it separates the groups by cell wall, so it narrows treatment choices quickly, unlike plain culture.
requirements.nearMiss: A Gram stain was used on the tap bacteria colonies because it is a quick technique that is widely used in labs.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives a reason, but the reason is general convenience. It is not the aim of separating Gram positive and Gram negative bacteria. So the technique is not linked to the outcome.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example connect the aim to the technique? Where does it compare with another method?

check.q: Which sentence justifies using a Gram stain on the tap bacteria?
options: A Gram stain was chosen because the aim was to separate the bacteria by cell wall type.
A Gram stain was chosen because it is a quick technique that is widely used in many labs.
A Gram stain was chosen because it shows the shape and size of the bacteria clearly.
A Gram stain was chosen because it identifies the exact species growing on the plate.
check.why: Justification links the technique to the outcome wanted, here separating Gram positive from Gram negative cells. 'Quick and widely used' is the tempting option because it sounds like a reason, but it describes the technique, not the aim.

requirements.need: Show you used techniques proficiently and document any changes you made.
requirements.fromSpec: Show how techniques were used proficiently; use observations and laboratory notebook evidence.
requirements.means: Your notebook and teacher observation are the evidence. Record what you changed and why, such as re-streaking a contaminated plate.
requirements.example: If a practical plate in the fictional lab became contaminated, a strong account would say what went wrong, which step was repeated with flamed loops, and how the learner's own record shows the aim was still met.
requirements.nearMiss: One plate became contaminated, so it was repeated with flamed loops and gave a clean result.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It records the fault and the fix. But it gives no cause. It does not show how the repeat kept the aim on track, so the reason for the change is missing.
requirements.explainPrompt: What evidence in the example shows proficiency (skilled work)? Why would the notebook entry matter to an assessor?

check.q: One plate became contaminated. Which record best shows proficient practical work?
options: A note that the plate was contaminated, then a clean repeat plate in the final results table.
A note of the likely cause, the repeat with flamed loops, and how the aim was still met.
A neat results table that leaves out the failed plate so that the report stays clear.
A copy of the method sheet showing the steps that the learner was meant to follow.
check.why: Proficiency is shown by recording what went wrong, what was changed and why the aim was still met. Leaving out the failed plate looks tidy, which is why it tempts, but it hides the evidence of skill and adaptation.

requirements.need: Make valid judgements about the risks and limits of techniques, and how they affect how useful the outcome is.
requirements.fromSpec: Make valid judgements about risks and limitations of techniques in relation to the usefulness of outcomes.
requirements.means: Think about what could go wrong or limit the result (fading stains, contamination, small samples). Say how that affects how far you can trust it.
requirements.example: A temporary stain fades within a day, so the slide cannot be rechecked by a colleague. In a hospital this would limit its use for a second opinion, so photographing the slide immediately is essential.
requirements.nearMiss: The stain faded within a day, so the slide could not be rechecked later. This is a limitation of the technique.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It states the limit and its direct effect. But it does not judge how much this matters for diagnosis. It does not say what would reduce the problem, such as photographing the slide.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example say the fading stain stops anyone doing? How does it fix this?

check.q: Which sentence makes a valid judgement about a limit of the technique?
options: The stain fades within a day, which is a limitation and a risk for the practical work.
A fading stain is a minor problem, because the colonies were already seen once by the group.
A fading stain stops colleagues rechecking the slide, so a photograph is needed at once.
A fading stain is the main limit of the method, and it was noticed within a day.
check.why: A valid judgement says what the limitation does to the usefulness of the result and what to do about it. Calling it a minor problem is a judgement, but it ignores the colleague's second opinion, so it is not valid.

requirements.need: Use the techniques and results to reach solutions as part of your justification.
requirements.fromSpec: Show how techniques and methods were used to arrive at solutions.
requirements.means: Finish with what your results told you and how the method got you there. Use peer results to explain odd outcomes.
requirements.example: In a serial dilution, growth that stops at the second-strongest disinfectant concentration would support recommending a dilution for the sink. Agreement between independent groups would make an error less likely, but only the learner's own results can be reported as theirs.
requirements.nearMiss: The disinfectant stopped growth at the second-strongest concentration, which suggests a dilution could be recommended for the sink.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It states a result and a recommendation. But it ignores the other groups' results. So it never checks if the finding is reliable or explains any difference.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why does the example mention the peer group? What would be less certain without it?

check.q: A group's serial dilution shows growth at a strength where other groups saw none. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Compare it with the other groups' results and suggest causes such as contamination.
Use the other groups' result instead, since agreement between groups shows who is correct.
Repeat the dilution until it matches the others, then report only that result.
Leave it out, because one unusual plate does not change the overall trend.
check.why: Unusual results should be reported as the learner's own and explained using peer data and possible causes. Adopting the peers' result is tempting because agreement looks reliable, but only your own results can be reported as yours.

requirements.need: Bring together the main processes and weigh their strengths and weaknesses.
requirements.fromSpec: Gather together main aspects of processes and techniques; evaluate strengths, weaknesses, advantages and disadvantages.
requirements.means: Compare the techniques side by side rather than describing them one at a time.
requirements.example: Culture identifies the organism and its antibiotic sensitivity but takes one to two days. A Gram stain is quick but gives less detail. Together they balance speed against certainty.
requirements.nearMiss: Culture takes one to two days and identifies the organism and its antibiotic sensitivity. A Gram stain is quick but gives less detail.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It compares the two correctly but stops there. It never says how speed trades off against certainty, or how the two work together.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does 'together they balance' tell you about how the example evaluates? Explain it in your own words.

check.q: Which sentence weighs culture against Gram staining?
options: Culture takes one to two days, but a Gram stain can be read within an hour or so.
A quick stain gives early information, while slower culture gives more certainty.
Culture and Gram staining are both common techniques that help to study bacteria.
Culture is better than Gram staining because it is the more thorough technique overall.
check.why: Evaluation shows the trade-off between speed and certainty. Timing each technique, the tempting option, compares facts but never says what the difference means for the doctor.

requirements.need: Link usefulness to a diagnosis that health professionals can act on.
requirements.fromSpec: Relate this to usefulness in providing a diagnosis that health care workers can use.
requirements.means: Ask how a doctor or nurse would use the result and whether it is fast, clear and reliable enough.
requirements.example: For the care home resident, a Gram stain result within hours would let the doctor start suitable treatment sooner. The full culture still matters because it checks the first choice was right.
requirements.nearMiss: For the care home resident, a Gram stain result within hours would help the doctor to start treatment sooner.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It links the result to speed and treatment. But it ignores reliability. It never says what the culture adds, or what could go wrong if the early result were used alone.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the doctor do differently because of the result? Say it in your own words.

check.q: What makes a result useful to the doctor treating the care home resident?
options: It contains detailed data about the organism, whether or not it arrives in time.
It has been checked and confirmed twice by the lab, even if this takes several days.
It matches what the doctor expected, so that no further tests are needed.
It is clear, timely and reliable enough for the doctor to decide on treatment.
check.why: Usefulness depends on whether a professional can act on the result. Detail and double-checking, the tempting options, improve quality, but a result that arrives late cannot help the resident.

requirements.need: Reach a valid overall judgement. Compare your practical work with commercial (professional) labs.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate and reach valid judgements, recognising limitations compared with a commercial laboratory.
requirements.means: End with a clear overall view and be honest about what a student lab cannot do.
requirements.example: College methods show the principles but lack the automation and controls of a hospital lab. Overall, staining plus culture is the most useful pair, though only the hospital's quality checks would make results safe for patients.
requirements.nearMiss: College methods show the principles of staining and culture, but a hospital lab has more automation and quality controls.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It compares the two settings correctly. But it gives no overall verdict on which technique is most useful, or what would make results safe for patients.
requirements.explainPrompt: What is the 'overall judgement' in the example? What evidence does it rest on?

check.q: Which final judgement is strongest in a report that compares college and hospital methods?
options: The hospital lab is better, because it has more equipment and trained staff than the college.
The college methods are as good as the hospital's, because both use agar and Gram stains.
Stain plus culture is most useful, but only hospital quality checks make results safe to use.
Both labs use useful methods, and each has strengths and weaknesses that were discussed earlier.
check.why: The strongest verdict chooses between the methods and gives a reason from the results and the comparison. Saying both labs have strengths and weaknesses, the tempting option, summarises but decides nothing.

parallelCase.title: Hollis and Amina in Ashbourne Reach
parallelCase.summary:
Setting: Ashbourne Reach, a fictional market town. It has a health centre and a small community hospital. It also has a day centre run by a local charity, and a home care agency.
Hollis Brandt, age 52: He is a self-employed barber with rheumatoid arthritis. His hands are swollen and stiff in the mornings, and he is tired most days.
What Hollis wants: He is worried about losing work. He wants to keep working and stay independent.
Hollis's tests so far: Blood tests and an X-ray of his hands.
Amina Rahman, age 70: She is a retired bus driver and lives with her husband, Tariq. A routine check showed her kidneys work at about half their normal level. This is chronic kidney disease.
Amina's health: She has no symptoms yet. She has high blood pressure and a family history of kidney problems.
What Amina wants: She dislikes taking many tablets. She is a practising Muslim and wants to keep fasting in Ramadan. Medicine and test times need planning with her doctor.
Amina's strengths: She makes her own decisions with confidence. She enjoys the day centre's craft group.
Amina's barriers: Hospital trips are hard because Tariq no longer drives. The town's community transport runs two mornings a week.
Tariq: He is her only regular carer and has a bad back.
The task: Write a care plan for Amina. It must suggest tests, treatment and support. These must fit her needs and the town's services. They must also fit the limits of what the options can achieve.

requirements.need: Judge how far each disorder affects body systems and daily life. Do not just name the effects.
requirements.fromSpec: Justify conclusions on the effects of different physiological disorders on body systems and functions.
requirements.means: Say which effects are most serious and why, rather than listing symptoms.
requirements.example: In rheumatoid arthritis the immune system attacks the joint lining, so pain and stiffness limit grip. For Hollis this matters most for his job, so the effect on work is probably greater than the pain itself.
requirements.nearMiss: In rheumatoid arthritis the immune system attacks the joint lining, causing pain, swelling and stiffness that limit grip and make barber's work harder for Hollis. Fatigue and worry add to this.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is accurate and applied to Hollis. But it lists effects side by side and never judges which matters most.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example judge to be the biggest effect? What word or phrase shows it is ranking rather than listing?

check.q: Which sentence judges rather than describes?
options: Rheumatoid arthritis damages Hollis's joints and makes his hands swollen and stiff in the mornings.
Hollis has swollen hands, tiredness and worry about work, and these are all symptoms of the disease.
Swollen, stiff joints are common in rheumatoid arthritis, according to the NHS, and affect Hollis.
Hollis's stiff hands matter more than the pain, because grip is how he earns a living.
check.why: Only the key ranks one effect above another and gives a reason. The tempting option applies the science accurately to Hollis but only describes it, which is the Merit-level trap of analysis without judgement.

requirements.need: Explain causes, signs and symptoms in depth and apply them to a less familiar situation.
requirements.fromSpec: Show in-depth understanding applied to less familiar situations of causes, signs and symptoms.
requirements.means: Use accurate science, then use it on an unusual case, such as a disease with no symptoms at first.
requirements.example: Chronic kidney disease often has no symptoms until late, so Amina feels well while her blood tests show damage. Her high blood pressure is both a possible cause and a result of the damage, so screening, not symptoms, is how it is found and monitored.
requirements.nearMiss: Amina's high blood pressure and family history raise her risk of chronic kidney disease, which damages the kidneys' filters. As it progresses she would be expected to feel tired and have swollen ankles.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It links cause to Amina but treats her as if she has symptoms. It misses that she feels well, which is the unusual feature to explain.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why is Amina's lack of symptoms important for how her condition is found? Say it in your own words.

check.q: Amina feels well but her kidneys work at about half normal. Which explanation shows in-depth understanding?
options: Chronic kidney disease can stay silent until late, so tests such as eGFR find it early.
The result must be wrong, because kidney disease always causes tiredness before the tests change.
Her kidneys cannot be damaged, because kidney disease would always cause pain in her back.
The damage comes from her age alone, so her high blood pressure plays no part in the disease.
check.why: Kidney damage can be silent, so routine tests find it before symptoms appear, which is the unusual feature here. The tempting 'tiredness first' option assumes symptoms must lead, which is not so in chronic kidney disease.

requirements.need: Apply the science to the second disorder rather than repeating the first.
requirements.fromSpec: Show in-depth understanding in less familiar situations for two different disorders.
requirements.means: Show how the causes and signs of each disorder differ, not just copy a template.
requirements.example: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disease, where the body's defences attack its own joints, so Hollis's symptoms are worse in the morning and come in flares. Amina's condition is a gradual loss of filtering, so her signs appear only when blood tests are repeated over months.
requirements.nearMiss: Hollis and Amina both have long-term conditions that affect how their bodies work and need regular care and appointments.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is true of both people. But it does not separate the cause or signs of either. It could be written without knowing either disorder.
requirements.explainPrompt: What differences between the two disorders does the example highlight? Why does that matter?

check.q: How do you show real understanding of two different disorders?
options: Describe both with the same headings and sentences, so that they can be compared directly.
Explain a cause or sign specific to each, such as autoimmune flares and silent decline.
Explain the general effects of long-term conditions, which apply equally to both people.
Use more medical terms in the first description, then refer back to it for the second.
check.why: Specific causes and signs for each disorder show understanding of both. Matching headings or general long-term effects, the tempting options, produce text that could be written without knowing either disorder.

requirements.need: Evaluate the impact on wellbeing and life, using local settings and research.
requirements.fromSpec: Use detailed analysis and research of local settings to make proposals for support.
requirements.means: Cover emotional, social and practical effects. Show you know what local services could do.
requirements.example: Hollis's worry about work may affect his mood as much as the pain. A local occupational therapist could adapt tools to keep him working, which would address the cause of his stress.
requirements.nearMiss: Hollis's rheumatoid arthritis affects him physically, emotionally and socially. He is worried about losing work and may feel low, and his tiredness could limit his social life.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It covers several areas of wellbeing. But it does not link any one to a local response, or say which effect matters most.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example connect Hollis's worry to practical help in his town?

check.q: What makes an impact evaluation detailed?
options: It uses longer sentences and more medical vocabulary to describe the person's condition.
It describes the worst outcome the condition could cause for the person, in full.
It covers body, mind and social life in turn, giving equal space to each.
It links effects on body, mind and social life and proposes a specific local response.
check.why: Depth comes from linking effects together and responding locally. Covering body, mind and social life in separate paragraphs is the tempting Merit-level answer: it is broad but never connects the effects or proposes a response.

requirements.need: Reach a short, professional overall judgement for each service user.
requirements.fromSpec: Articulate arguments and views concisely and professionally to justify conclusions.
requirements.means: Finish with a short judgement that says which impact matters most and what it depends on.
requirements.example: Overall, Hollis's disorder affects his work and independence more than his life expectancy, while Amina's affects her future health more than her daily life. So support for Hollis should be quick and practical, and for Amina it should be steady and preventive.
requirements.nearMiss: In conclusion, both disorders have a big impact on the lives of Hollis and Amina and affect their health and wellbeing in many ways.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is a polite summary. But it makes no difference between the two people and gives no basis for decisions.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the final judgement say that differs between the two people? Why does it matter for support?

check.q: Which closing sentence is a justified conclusion?
options: Both conditions are serious and long-term, so both people need regular care and support from services.
Hollis needs quick practical help to work, whereas Amina needs steady monitoring, as impacts differ.
Rheumatoid arthritis and chronic kidney disease are different disorders with quite different effects.
Hollis is more affected than Amina, because his disorder has symptoms that hers does not have.
check.why: A justified conclusion distinguishes the two people and says why. The tempting 'both are serious' option is accurate but decides nothing, and the ranking option rests on symptoms alone, which is not a reasoned basis for support.

requirements.need: Justify the choice of investigations (tests) for each disorder, using what they show.
requirements.fromSpec: Draw on knowledge of investigative and diagnostic procedures, making suitable justifications.
requirements.means: Say what each test shows, why it was chosen and what its limits are.
requirements.example: An eGFR blood test shows how well Amina's kidneys filter, and a urine test for protein shows damage. Together they are less invasive than a scan and track change over time.
requirements.nearMiss: Amina had a blood test (eGFR) and a urine test for protein. The blood test measures how well the kidneys filter and the urine test shows whether the kidneys are leaking protein.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It says what each test measures, which is good. But it gives no reason these tests were chosen over others, and no limit.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does each test tell the doctor in the example? Which words turn that into a justification?

check.q: Which sentence justifies an investigation?
options: An eGFR test is a blood test that measures kidney filtering, and it was done on Amina.
Blood tests are the most common investigation in health care, so one suits Amina well.
An eGFR test shows kidney filtering and can be repeated cheaply to track change.
A kidney biopsy gives the most accurate answer, so it is the best choice for Amina.
check.why: Justification says why a test fits this person, here its low cost and use for tracking change. Saying what a test measures, the tempting Merit-level option, describes the test without explaining why it was chosen over others.

requirements.need: Show you understand the limits of tests and why more than one is needed.
requirements.fromSpec: Draw on knowledge of investigative and diagnostic procedures, making suitable justifications.
requirements.means: State what a test cannot show, and which second test fills the gap.
requirements.example: A blood test for rheumatoid factor can be negative in some people with rheumatoid arthritis and positive in some without it. So Hollis's diagnosis also depends on his symptoms, inflammation markers and an X-ray of his hands.
requirements.nearMiss: Hollis had a blood test for rheumatoid factor and an X-ray of his hands. The blood test looks for an antibody linked to rheumatoid arthritis and the X-ray looks for joint damage.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It says what each test looks for. But it does not say that one result alone can mislead, so it never justifies using both.
requirements.explainPrompt: What is the limit of the blood test in the example? How does that justify the other tests?

check.q: A single eGFR reading for Amina is lower than normal. What should happen next?
options: Repeat the test after about three months and add a urine test, since results vary.
Diagnose chronic kidney disease straight away, because eGFR is a reliable test on its own.
Ignore the result for now, because she feels well and has no symptoms to explain it.
Order a kidney biopsy immediately, because it is the most accurate test of kidney damage.
check.why: Chronic kidney disease is confirmed by repeated results over time with a urine test. Diagnosing from one reading is the tempting option, but it ignores that a single result can vary and that the limits of a test are why more than one is needed.

requirements.need: Justify treatment options. Give benefits and drawbacks.
requirements.fromSpec: Justify the potential benefits of treatment options.
requirements.means: Compare options and say which suits the person and why, including drawbacks.
requirements.example: Blood pressure medication slows damage to Amina's kidneys, so it is a priority. Its disadvantage is more tablets, which she dislikes, so the plan needs a simple routine.
requirements.nearMiss: Blood pressure medication helps to protect Amina's kidneys, but it can cause side effects, so her doctor will review it regularly.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names a benefit and a drawback. But it does not weigh them for Amina or link them to her dislike of tablets.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why does the example state a disadvantage? How does that help make a recommendation?

check.q: What does justifying a treatment involve?
options: Listing every drug that could treat the condition, with its usual dose and timing.
Stating that doctors recommend the treatment, since they are trained to decide.
Explaining how the drug works inside the body to produce its beneficial effect.
Weighing the benefits against the drawbacks for this particular person.
check.why: Justification weighs benefit against drawback for the individual. Explaining how a drug works, the tempting option, is accurate science, but it describes the mechanism and never reasons about whether the treatment suits this person.

requirements.need: Compare the treatment for two different disorders, including how their aims differ.
requirements.fromSpec: Make suitable justifications of treatment options for two different disorders.
requirements.means: Say what each treatment is trying to achieve, and why that differs.
requirements.example: Hollis's treatment aims to control inflammation early and keep him working, so disease-modifying drugs and physiotherapy are justified, though they need regular blood monitoring. Amina's aims to slow decline, so controlling blood pressure and diet is justified over more invasive options.
requirements.nearMiss: Hollis may be given drugs and physiotherapy for rheumatoid arthritis, and Amina may be given blood pressure medication and diet advice for chronic kidney disease.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names likely treatments for each person but not the aim of each. So it does not justify why these suit their disorders.
requirements.explainPrompt: What is the aim of each treatment in the example? Why does the aim differ?

check.q: Why do the treatment plans for Hollis and Amina look different?
options: Each plan aims at a different outcome: control inflammation and work, or slow decline.
Hollis is younger than Amina, so he needs more medicine to control his condition.
One condition is more serious than the other, so it needs a stronger treatment plan.
Both are long-term conditions, so both plans should aim to control symptoms in the same way.
check.why: Plans differ because their aims differ. The tempting 'same aim' option treats all long-term conditions alike, and the age and seriousness options rest on assumptions that do not set treatment.

requirements.need: Use research on local settings, care types and carers to propose provision.
requirements.fromSpec: Use detailed analysis and research of local settings to propose treatment, support, carers and care settings.
requirements.means: Name the kinds of services and carers available locally. Explain which fit each service user.
requirements.example: Hollis could use the community hospital's physiotherapy and the day centre's peer group. Amina's husband is her main informal carer, but the agency could help with transport.
requirements.nearMiss: Ashbourne Reach has a health centre, a community hospital, a day centre and a home care agency, and these could support Hollis and Amina with their conditions.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It lists the services correctly but matches none to a need. It shows research but not application.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example match each service to a person? Why is that better than listing?

check.q: Which is the strongest use of local research?
options: Listing every service in the town, with what each one offers in general.
Giving a general conclusion that the town's services are good overall.
Matching a named local service to a need that was identified earlier.
Quoting national research on carers without saying what the town provides.
check.why: Matching shows research applied. Listing every service, the tempting Merit-level option, presents information without choosing, and national research alone is not local.

requirements.need: Justify the choice of carers and care settings, including the strain on informal carers (unpaid family or friends).
requirements.fromSpec: Use research to propose types of carers and care settings for two service users.
requirements.means: Compare informal and formal carers and say what support the carer needs.
requirements.example: Tariq is Amina's only regular carer and has a bad back, so relying on him for hospital trips is risky. A carer's assessment and community transport on two mornings a week would protect his health and keep her appointments.
requirements.nearMiss: Amina's husband Tariq looks after her at home, and the home care agency could also help. Formal and informal carers both have a role.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names both kinds of carer but ignores the strain on Tariq. So it does not justify any change to the arrangement.
requirements.explainPrompt: What problem with the current carer does the example spot? How does the proposal address it?

check.q: Why should a care plan consider the informal carer's own needs?
options: Because informal carers are paid by the council and so need contracts and rights.
Because the arrangement may fail if the carer's own health or time is stretched.
Because informal carers usually want to stop caring and need a replacement found.
Because the plan is judged only on the service user's needs, not on the carer's.
check.why: Plans fail when carers are overstretched, so the carer's strain belongs in the plan. The 'service user only' option is tempting because the plan is about Amina, but it ignores that her care depends on Tariq.

requirements.need: Choose the most appropriate options within the constraints and desired outcomes.
requirements.fromSpec: Make the most appropriate selections within given constraints and desired outcomes.
requirements.means: State the constraints (limits such as transport, tablets and budget) and choose to fit them.
requirements.example: Because Amina's husband no longer drives, blood tests at the health centre rather than the hospital fit her ability to attend and still give the data needed.
requirements.nearMiss: Amina should have regular blood tests at the health centre, because they show how well her kidneys are working.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives a sensible test and reason, but never names the constraint (no driver) that makes the health centre the best choice.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which constraint shapes the choice in the example?

check.q: What is a constraint in a care plan?
options: A target the plan aims to reach, such as steadier blood pressure.
A symptom or sign that the person has and the plan must reduce.
Something that limits what is possible, such as transport or time.
A treatment that the plan uses, such as a drug or a change of diet.
check.why: A constraint limits the choices open to the planner. The tempting 'target' option confuses a constraint with an outcome, and symptoms and treatments are parts of the condition or the plan, not limits on it.

requirements.need: Match solutions to barriers, or show new thinking.
requirements.fromSpec: Use knowledge to match solutions to potential barriers or innovate and show lateral thinking.
requirements.means: Identify what might stop the plan working and solve it, perhaps in a creative way.
requirements.example: Amina dislikes taking many tablets, so the pharmacy could provide a weekly pill organiser and one check-in call, which keeps the treatment without adding pressure.
requirements.nearMiss: Amina dislikes tablets, so her doctor should explain why each medicine matters and review whether all of them are needed.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is a sensible response, but a standard one. It does not adapt the routine to her barrier or use a local service.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example turn a barrier into an action?

check.q: Which is the most innovative (new and creative) response to Amina disliking tablets?
options: Telling her she must take every tablet or her kidneys will fail quickly.
Using a weekly pill organiser and one check-in call from the pharmacy.
Prescribing extra tablets as back-up in case she misses some doses.
Giving her a leaflet that explains each tablet and why it matters.
check.why: A tailored routine tackles the barrier without adding pressure. The leaflet is the tempting standard response: sensible, but it does not adapt the routine, while threats cause anxiety and extra tablets worsen the barrier.

requirements.need: Judge the limitations of the methods compared with the outcomes wanted.
requirements.fromSpec: Make valid judgements about limitations of methods in relation to desired outcomes.
requirements.means: No treatment is perfect. State what the plan cannot achieve and what happens next.
requirements.example: Medication and diet slow kidney decline but cannot restore lost function. So the plan includes reviewing her blood results every few months and discussing future options with her specialist.
requirements.nearMiss: The plan should slow Amina's kidney decline, though it may not work for everyone, so her progress will be reviewed.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It hints that the plan may fail but does not say what it cannot achieve or what would be done if it does.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example admit the plan cannot do? Why does that make it stronger?

check.q: Why include limitations in a plan?
options: They show realistic judgement and let the plan prepare for change.
They protect the planner, because failure can then be blamed on the condition.
They show that the plan is weak, so a stronger one should be written instead.
They are required by law for any plan about a long-term condition.
check.why: Honest limits support valid judgement and lead to review points. The 'protect the planner' option is tempting but treats limits as an excuse, and admitting limits does not make a plan weak or satisfy a legal rule.

requirements.need: Show how consent and confidentiality shape the plan.
requirements.fromSpec: Respect confidentiality at all times and obtain formal consent from service users to report any information.
requirements.means: Explain how you protect the service user's identity and record their agreement. Do this before you use their details.
requirements.example: For Hollis, the plan would use a made-up name and leave out his workplace, because a barber in a small town could be identified. His written agreement would be kept before any personal detail was used.
requirements.nearMiss: Hollis's details will be kept private and he has been told how the information will be used.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It states the right intention, but gives no step that protects identity and no record of consent.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which details in the example could identify Hollis? What is done about them?

check.q: Which action best respects consent (agreement) and confidentiality (keeping details private)?
options: Using the person's real name, because the planner already knows them well.
Getting agreement once, verbally, and keeping no written record of it.
Asking a family member to agree instead, since they know the person's wishes.
Changing identifying details and keeping a signed consent form on file.
check.why: Formal consent and a protected identity are both needed. Verbal agreement is the tempting option because the person did agree, but it leaves no record, and knowing someone or asking a relative does not replace consent.

requirements.need: Show the factors considered when planning, and how plans are modified.
requirements.fromSpec: Use knowledge to plan treatment, including the factors that need to be considered, and modify to deal with contingencies.
requirements.means: Name the factors (age, preferences and beliefs, other conditions, money, carers). Say what you would change if something went wrong.
requirements.example: For Amina, age, high blood pressure, a carer with a bad back and a dislike of tablets all shape the plan. If her blood results fall faster than expected, the plan would bring forward the specialist review.
requirements.nearMiss: Amina is 70 and has high blood pressure, so her plan includes blood pressure treatment and regular tests.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It uses two factors but not carer, preference or money. It says nothing about what changes if the plan does not work.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which factors does the example use? What would trigger a change to the plan?

check.q: What does it mean to plan for a contingency?
options: To choose the cheapest option, so that the plan stays within budget.
To prepare what will change if the plan does not work as hoped.
To leave risks out of the plan, so that it does not worry the person.
To repeat the same plan every month until the person's condition improves.
check.why: Contingency planning prepares alternatives in advance. The cheapest option is the tempting confusion, since it is a constraint, and leaving out risks or repeating an unchanged plan ignores the need to adapt.

parallelCase.title: Tidewater Spa and Residential Home
parallelCase.summary:
Setting: Tidewater, a fictional coastal hotel. It has a hydrotherapy pool, a kitchen and a wing of rooms for older residents.
Problem 1: A routine test of the showers finds Legionella. This is a bacterium that lives in warm water systems.
Problem 2: Three kitchen staff develop sickness and diarrhoea. Norovirus, a virus, is suspected.
What the manager must do: She must decide how to control each microorganism.
Her wider reading: She is reading how diseases such as dengue and cholera now spread across countries more easily. The causes are air travel, trade, city growth and a changing climate.
What she wants to know: What the consequences of a global outbreak would be. This includes the effects on health workers and on fairness in access to treatment.
Helpful microbes: The kitchen makes sourdough and kefir with live microbes. Some residents take antibiotics. So she wants a balanced view of humans and microorganisms.

requirements.need: Use several sources of information. Compare how to control two different microorganisms.
requirements.fromSpec: Draw on a number of information sources about microbe control methods for two different micro-organisms.
requirements.means: Use more than one reliable source for each microbe and compare what they say.
requirements.example: Public health guidance and a hospital infection-control guide both advise keeping hot water above a set temperature to control Legionella. Two sources agreeing makes the method more credible.
requirements.nearMiss: A health protection agency page and a hospital guide both explain how to control Legionella in water systems, and both were used to describe the methods.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Two sources are used, but they are not compared or weighed, so the answer reports rather than judges.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why does agreement between two sources make the example stronger? What would you check if they disagreed?

check.q: How do several sources show breadth?
options: By reading one long, detailed source carefully and quoting it throughout.
By using a different source for each point and describing each in turn.
By relying on one clear video that covers both microbes in a short clip.
By comparing reliable sources and noting where they agree or differ.
check.why: Comparing reliable sources shows breadth and judgement. Using a different source for each point is the tempting Merit-level option: it spreads sources out but never weighs them against each other.

requirements.need: Give reasons why some control methods are used and others are not.
requirements.fromSpec: Come to a supported judgement and give reasons why some are used and not others.
requirements.means: Say why a method suits one microbe and not another, or this setting.
requirements.example: Alcohol hand gel is weak against norovirus, so handwashing with soap and water and cleaning with chlorine-based products are preferred. Gel alone would leave the kitchen at risk.
requirements.nearMiss: Soap and water and alcohol gel are both used to control microbes in the kitchen, and chlorine products are used on surfaces. Soap and water are better than gel in many cases.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It prefers one method but does not explain why it works better against norovirus. So the preference is stated, not justified.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example say about alcohol gel and norovirus? Why does that decide the method?

check.q: Why might a control method not be used for a particular microbe?
options: It is old, so it is likely to be out of date and unsafe to use.
It is cheap, so it is unlikely to be effective enough for the job.
It may not work against that microbe or in that setting.
It is used for other microbes, so it cannot work on this one.
check.why: Methods are chosen because of their effect on the microbe and the setting. Age, cost and use against other microbes do not decide effectiveness, and alcohol gel shows this, as it works on many microbes but poorly on norovirus.

requirements.need: Link the control method to the microbe's biology, such as whether it can grow outside a host.
requirements.fromSpec: Reach a supported judgement drawing on information sources about microbe control.
requirements.means: Explain what the method removes or damages and why that affects this microbe.
requirements.example: Legionella multiplies in warm, stagnant water, so keeping hot water hot and flushing little-used outlets removes the conditions it needs. Norovirus is a virus that cannot multiply in water or on surfaces, so temperature control would not help; cleaning and excluding sick staff are the controls.
requirements.nearMiss: Legionella is a bacterium and norovirus is a virus, so they need different methods. Water temperature control is used for Legionella and hygiene for norovirus.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names the right methods for each microbe but does not explain, from their biology, why those methods fit.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does Legionella need that temperature control removes? Why does the same method not help for norovirus?

check.q: Why does controlling the water temperature not control norovirus?
options: Norovirus is a virus that cannot multiply outside a host, so heating water does not limit it.
Norovirus is a bacterium that prefers cold water, so heating the water would not affect it at all.
Norovirus is killed by antibiotics, so temperature control is not needed to deal with it at all.
Norovirus is a virus, and viruses cannot be controlled by any method outside a hospital setting.
check.why: Viruses only multiply inside host cells, so water temperature cannot limit norovirus as it limits Legionella. The tempting bacterium and antibiotic options confuse viruses with bacteria.

requirements.need: Reach a justified conclusion. Use short, professional language.
requirements.fromSpec: Articulate arguments concisely and professionally to reach justified conclusions.
requirements.means: Finish with a clear view on the best control method for each microbe, with brief reasons.
requirements.example: For Legionella, temperature control and flushing outlets are most reliable since the bacteria multiply in warm, stagnant water. For norovirus, hygiene and exclusion of sick staff are best because it spreads person to person.
requirements.nearMiss: In conclusion, microbes are controlled by hot water temperatures, flushing, hand washing and cleaning, and each has a role at Tidewater.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It lists the methods but never chooses a best one for each microbe or says why.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which words in the example make it a justified conclusion?

check.q: A good conclusion includes:
options: A summary of every method discussed, in the order that they appeared.
A balanced list of the strengths and weaknesses of each method.
A recommendation to use all of the methods together, to be safe.
A named best method for each microbe, with a brief reason.
check.why: A clear choice with a reason is a justified conclusion. The balanced list of strengths and weaknesses is the tempting Merit-level option, as it analyses each method but never chooses one.

requirements.need: Give a clear and objective account of why disease is spreading globally.
requirements.fromSpec: Give a clear, objective account of reasons for outbreaks becoming global.
requirements.means: Name several causes (travel, trade, urban living, climate) and explain how each helps a named disease spread.
requirements.example: Dengue is carried by mosquitoes whose range grows as temperatures rise, while air travel lets infected people move before symptoms show. Together these explain faster spread.
requirements.nearMiss: Dengue is spreading to new countries because of climate change and global travel, which are both increasing, and this is a growing public health problem.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names two causes but not how either works, so the account asserts rather than explains.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which two causes does the example link to dengue? Why do they matter together?

check.q: What makes an account of global spread objective?
options: It rests on evidence and reasons, and keeps opinion out of the account.
It uses strong adjectives to show how serious the global spread has become.
It includes a personal story about one outbreak to show its human effects.
It uses short, simple sentences so that every point is easy to follow.
check.why: Objective means evidence-based. Strong adjectives, personal stories and short sentences change the tone or readability, but none of them makes an account more objective.

requirements.need: Rank the causes of global spread and judge which matter most.
requirements.fromSpec: Use breadth of information across learning aims B and C to critically discuss why diseases are spreading more frequently on a global scale.
requirements.means: Compare the causes and say which has the largest effect for a named disease, and why.
requirements.example: For cholera, urban crowding and poor sanitation probably matter more than air travel, because the disease spreads through contaminated water. For dengue, travel and climate matter more, because the vector and the infected people move.
requirements.nearMiss: Travel, trade, urbanisation and climate change all increase the spread of disease, and cholera and dengue are examples of this.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It lists causes correctly and names diseases. But it weighs none of them, so the 'critical' element is missing.
requirements.explainPrompt: What reason does the example give for ranking different causes for different diseases?

check.q: Which statement is a critical discussion of the causes of global spread?
options: Air travel spreads all diseases equally quickly, so it ranks first for every outbreak.
The most important cause depends on the route: water for cholera, travel for dengue.
Climate change is the only real reason that diseases now spread more widely.
Travel, trade, urban growth and climate all contribute to the spread of disease.
check.why: Ranking causes by the disease's route is critical discussion. Listing travel, trade, urban growth and climate is the tempting Merit-level option: it is accurate, but it weighs none of them.

requirements.need: Describe what a pandemic (a disease spreading across many countries) would probably do. Cover individuals, families, societies and health workers.
requirements.fromSpec: Describe likely consequences including effects on individuals, families and health workers.
requirements.means: Cover different groups. Include health workers and how society feels about the disease.
requirements.example: In a cholera pandemic, families might lose a wage earner, and health workers face infection risk and long hours. Fear can lead communities to stigmatise sufferers, which makes people hide symptoms.
requirements.nearMiss: In a pandemic many people become ill and some die, families are affected, and hospitals and health workers are under pressure.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names several groups but gives each one line. It does not link them or show how they affect control of the disease.
requirements.explainPrompt: Name the groups in the example. Why does stigma matter for control?

check.q: Which statement best describes what a pandemic does to different groups?
options: Many people become ill and some die, so families and societies are affected as well.
Health workers face infection risk because they spend long hours treating the sick.
Fear of stigma makes sufferers hide symptoms, which makes control harder for health workers.
Pandemics mainly affect the individuals who are ill, since other groups are not directly harmed.
check.why: Describing consequences well shows how effects on one group reach another. The tempting 'many become ill' option names groups in a single line, and the health worker option is true but covers one group alone.

requirements.need: Discuss the ethical issues of using tested and untested treatments.
requirements.fromSpec: Consider whether tested and untested drugs will be used, and the ethical dilemmas raised.
requirements.means: Explain the dilemma: hope of benefit versus risk and fairness.
requirements.example: In an outbreak with no proven treatment, giving an untested drug may save lives but could also cause harm. Fair access is a second dilemma, since limited doses must be shared.
requirements.nearMiss: Untested drugs could help people in an outbreak but may be unsafe, so some people think they should not be used and others think they should.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It states both sides but does not say what makes it a dilemma or mention fairness, so it stops at 'some say'.
requirements.explainPrompt: What are the two dilemmas in the example? Explain them in your own words.

check.q: Which situation is an ethical dilemma (a hard choice where each option has a cost)?
options: Deciding which of two proven treatments is cheaper for the hospital to buy this year.
Deciding to give a proven treatment to a patient who has agreed to take the treatment.
Deciding which hospital to send a patient to when both offer exactly the same treatment.
Deciding whether to give an untested drug that might save lives but could cause harm.
