check.why: A dilemma balances competing benefits and harms, as with an untested drug. The other options are practical choices or decisions where no right or risk is in conflict.

requirements.need: Show you understand different attitudes in society and the position of health workers.
requirements.fromSpec: Consider the position of health workers dealing with the outbreak and sensitivity to different societal attitudes.
requirements.means: Explain how beliefs and customs affect control. Say how workers should respond with respect.
requirements.example: In some communities traditional burial practices involve close contact with the body, which can spread infection. Health workers who explain the risk and agree safe alternatives with community leaders are more likely to be trusted than those who simply forbid the practice.
requirements.nearMiss: Different communities have different attitudes and beliefs about disease, and health workers should be sensitive when dealing with an outbreak.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It states the idea but gives no example of an attitude or response. So it cannot be applied.
requirements.explainPrompt: What attitude does the example mention? How should health workers respond?

check.q: Why is respect for local beliefs important during an outbreak?
options: It is a matter of politeness only and makes little difference to control.
People who feel respected are more likely to follow safety advice.
It allows health workers to set aside the science where beliefs differ.
It means every local belief should be followed, even if it spreads infection.
check.why: Trust improves cooperation, so respect has a practical effect on control. Respect is not just politeness, does not replace evidence, and does not mean giving up safe practice.

requirements.need: Use research from both learning aims to discuss critically why global spread is increasing.
requirements.fromSpec: Use breadth of information across B and C to critically discuss why diseases spread more frequently globally.
requirements.means: Link transmission (how it spreads), immunity and control to global conditions. Focus on control across the world, not one country.
requirements.example: Control at global level is harder than in one country because borders, health systems and vaccine supply differ. This explains why an outbreak controlled locally can still return.
requirements.nearMiss: Countries work together to control outbreaks by sharing information and vaccines, and control methods are useful in outbreaks.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is true, but treats global control as a simple version of local control. It shows no obstacles or differences.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example say makes global control harder?

check.q: Why is global control different from controlling an outbreak in one country?
options: Diseases become weaker as they spread to countries far from the source.
Travel stops during outbreaks, so countries manage the disease separately.
Countries have different resources, rules and access to vaccines.
Global control is the same as local control, only across more people.
check.why: Global control depends on coordination between unequal health systems. The tempting 'same, only bigger' option treats it as simple local control scaled up, which ignores differences between countries.

requirements.need: Present facts on both the good and bad effects of human-microbe relationships.
requirements.fromSpec: The interrelationship can have positive and negative effects; present the facts.
requirements.means: Give real examples of benefits and harms, such as gut bacteria and infections.
requirements.example: Gut bacteria help digest food and compete with harmful microbes, but some of the same species can cause infection if they enter the wrong part of the body.
requirements.nearMiss: Microbes can be beneficial, such as in food production and digestion, and harmful, such as in infections, so the relationship has both positives and negatives.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It has both sides, but gives categories not specific facts, so nothing can be checked.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example show the same microbes can be good and harmful?

check.q: Which statement is a fact that can be checked, about a benefit of microbes?
options: Kefir is made when live bacteria and yeasts ferment milk into a drink.
Microbes are beneficial in many areas of life, including food and health.
Beneficial microbes are more important to people than harmful microbes.
Most microbes help people, so the relationship is mainly positive.
check.why: A fact is specific and checkable, and kefir fermentation can be checked. Saying microbes are beneficial in many areas, the tempting option, names a category with no fact behind it.

requirements.need: Judge whether the relationship is good overall. Back your arguments with facts.
requirements.fromSpec: Use facts to interpret whether the interrelationship is of overall benefit or not; a definite conclusion is not required.
requirements.means: Weigh the evidence. You may conclude 'it depends', but say what it depends on.
requirements.example: Fermented foods and gut bacteria support health daily, while serious infections are rarer but more severe. The benefit appears greater, although antibiotic resistance could shift the balance.
requirements.nearMiss: Microbes bring both benefits, such as food and digestion, and harms, such as disease, so the overall effect depends on the microbe and the situation.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It says 'it depends' but not on what, and does not weigh frequency or severity.
requirements.explainPrompt: What facts does the example use to weigh the balance?

check.q: Must you reach a definite conclusion about whether the relationship is beneficial?
options: Yes, a clear verdict is always required, even when the facts are mixed.
No, because a balanced description of both sides is enough on its own.
Yes, but only if it is a view that most scientists would accept.
Not always, but any view that is given must be argued with facts.
check.why: The guidance accepts a balanced view if it is backed by facts. The balanced description option is tempting but stops at 'it depends'; 'always' and 'consensus only' go beyond the guidance.

requirements.need: Draw on knowledge from across the unit to support your judgement.
requirements.fromSpec: Draw on knowledge gained across the unit to reach supported judgements.
requirements.means: Link back to control methods, disease spread and immunity.
requirements.example: Antibiotic use controls infection but also affects the helpful gut bacteria and encourages resistance. This links control (A) with the benefit and harm of microbes (D).
requirements.nearMiss: Antibiotics are helpful because they kill bacteria that cause disease, and they are used in hospitals and homes like Tidewater.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives one use of antibiotics. It does not link to resistance or gut bacteria. So no other part of the unit is used.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which other part of the unit does the example connect to?

check.q: Why link ideas across the unit when judging microbes?
options: It makes the answer longer, which shows that the topic has been covered.
It repeats earlier learning, which proves that it has been remembered.
It shows how different parts of the topic affect each other.
It shows wider reading, because each linked topic needs its own source.
check.why: Linking shows synthesis: antibiotics connect control with the benefits and harms of microbes. Length, repetition and extra sources add words, not understanding.

requirements.need: Discuss the good that microbes do and how they might be used in future.
requirements.fromSpec: Discuss the importance of useful microbes, their social benefits and possible future uses.
requirements.means: Give a current use, its benefit to people, and one realistic future use.
requirements.example: Bacteria are used to make insulin and yeast to make bread, so their benefit is large and everyday. A future use could be microbes that clean oil spills, but this is still being developed, so the claim is cautious.
requirements.nearMiss: Microbes are used to make food, medicines and cleaning products, and in the future they might be used for many more things.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names uses but gives no example or benefit, and the future claim is vague.
requirements.explainPrompt: What is the current benefit in the example? How does it keep the future claim cautious?

check.q: What makes a claim about future uses of microbes credible?
options: It is based on current research and openly acknowledges what is uncertain.
It is stated with certainty, so that it sounds more convincing to a reader.
It uses scientific terms without explanation, so that it sounds more expert.
It describes the most exciting possible use first, to catch the reader's interest.
check.why: Credible claims link to current research and admit what is still being developed. Certainty, technical vocabulary and excitement make a claim sound strong without making it supported.

parallelCase.title: Fenhaven Young Carers and Quayside Surgery
parallelCase.summary:
Setting: Fenhaven, a fictional coastal town.
Fenhaven Young Carers Project: A small charity for children and teenagers who look after a parent or sibling. It runs after-school clubs, helps with school liaison (working with schools) and offers breaks. It is funded by short grants and a local authority contract.
Quayside Surgery: A nearby GP practice. It is commissioned through the Integrated Care Board (formerly the Clinical Commissioning Group).
Laws staff follow: The Children and Families Act 2014, the Care Act 2014, the Equality Act 2010 and data protection law.
Codes of practice: Workers also follow professional codes, such as the standards set by Social Work England for registered social workers.
What is happening this year: The charity's grant is ending. A newspaper has run a story about hidden young carers. A national charity has published a report calling for earlier identification.
What the practice must do: Keep a young carers register.
The task: Judge how government policy and other factors shape each setting's work for young carers. Judge how law and codes affect staff and service users. Judge whether policy has improved wellbeing.

requirements.need: Evaluate the policy-making process and the government's role. Do not just describe the steps.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate and reach reasoned judgements on the background to policy making and the role of government affecting one local setting.
requirements.means: Weigh up how well policy gets from national government to local practice. Say what that means for the setting.
requirements.example: Government sets duties in law and funds them through departments and local authorities. For Fenhaven, this means the young carers' duty is national, but the money is local and short-term, so the policy's effect depends on grants.
requirements.nearMiss: Parliament passes the Children and Families Act 2014, which gives young carers a right to assessment, and local authorities carry out the duty.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It describes accurately how a national duty reaches local level. But it never judges how well the process works for Fenhaven, for example the effect of short-term local funding.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example say about the gap between national duties and local money? Explain why this is a judgement.

check.q: Which statement evaluates the policy-making process, not just describes it?
options: Parliament passes Acts, and local authorities then carry out the duties that they set.
National duties are only as effective as the local funding that delivers them.
Government departments lead policy, while local authorities run services for young carers.
The Children and Families Act 2014 gave young carers a right to an assessment.
check.why: Evaluation judges how well the process works in practice, here by tying national duties to local funding. The tempting description of Parliament and local authorities is accurate but only outlines the steps.

requirements.need: Judge the factors that influence policy (such as funding, media, pressure groups and research).
requirements.fromSpec: Draw on the factors that influence policy making, making suitable justifications.
requirements.means: Choose the most influential factors for your setting and say why they matter more than others.
requirements.example: The national charity's report and the newspaper story have raised the profile of hidden young carers. Funding is more influential locally, because without a grant the project cannot act on the attention.
requirements.nearMiss: The national charity's report and the newspaper story raised the profile of hidden young carers, and the grant ending threatens the project's funding.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names three real factors from the case, but never ranks them or says which matters most, so influence is described but not judged.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why does the example rank funding above the media? Do you agree?

check.q: Which statement judges the weight of the factors that influence policy on young carers?
options: A newspaper story and a national charity report both helped to influence policy on young carers.
Media coverage is the strongest factor, because a story reaches more people than a report does.
All the factors matter equally, because policy responds to funding, media and pressure groups.
Funding matters more locally than media coverage, as without a grant the project cannot act.
check.why: A judged ranking says which factor matters most and why, in this case. Naming the newspaper story and the charity report, the tempting option, identifies factors but gives them no weight.

requirements.need: Show how policy affects practice in the local setting, for one specific service user need.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate how practice of a local setting is affected by government policy in meeting a specific need of a service user group.
requirements.means: Pick one need (for example, finding hidden young carers). Follow the policy through to what workers actually do.
requirements.example: The duty to assess young carers means Quayside must identify them. A register helps, but busy receptionists may miss clues, so the policy only works if staff are trained to ask.
requirements.nearMiss: The duty to assess young carers means Quayside keeps a young carers register to identify them.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It links the duty to the register. But it does not judge how well the register meets the need, for example whether staff are trained to spot young carers.
requirements.explainPrompt: What problem does the example find when policy becomes practice?

check.q: Which answer best links policy to practice at Quayside Surgery?
options: Quayside has a young carers register, which shows that it follows the policy.
The duty to assess leads to a register, which works only if staff are trained to ask.
The Children and Families Act 2014 sets out the duty to assess young carers at Quayside.
Quayside must follow the Act, so its practice meets the needs of every young carer.
check.why: A strong link traces the route from duty to staff action and notes where it may fail. Having a register, the tempting option, shows an action was taken but assumes that this means the duty is met.

requirements.need: Use secondary research (research by others). Judge whether an organisation's priorities match what service users need.
requirements.fromSpec: Use secondary research to justify the validity of organisations' priorities in representing service users' needs.
requirements.means: Compare what an organisation says its priorities are with what research says service users need.
requirements.example: Research from national carers' charities suggests young carers most want to be recognised at school. Fenhaven's priority of school liaison therefore matches need well, although its grant limits how many it can reach.
requirements.nearMiss: Fenhaven offers after-school clubs, school liaison and breaks. Research from national carers' charities suggests young carers most want to be recognised at school.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Both the research and Fenhaven's services are correct, but they are not compared. So it never judges whether the priorities match what young carers need.
requirements.explainPrompt: What evidence tests Fenhaven's priority? Why is secondary research suitable here?

check.q: Which is the best use of secondary research to test Fenhaven's priorities?
options: Comparing a national carers' charity report on young carers' wants with Fenhaven's priorities.
Interviewing young carers at the project about what they want from the service it offers.
Describing Fenhaven's clubs, school liaison and breaks from the project's own leaflet and website.
Quoting a newspaper story about hidden young carers without checking where it got its facts.
check.why: Secondary research is published work by others, here used to test the priorities against need. Interviewing young carers is tempting because it asks them directly, but it is primary research, a different thing.

requirements.need: Evaluate how legislation and codes of practice affect workers in two settings.
requirements.fromSpec: Reach original and valid conclusions about how policy and codes affect individuals working in two different settings.
requirements.means: Describe what the law and codes require of staff, then judge how helpful or difficult that is in each setting.
requirements.example: A registered social worker must follow professional standards, which gives clear boundaries but adds recording work. A GP receptionist's duty to protect data is similar but less specialised, so training matters more.
requirements.nearMiss: A registered social worker must follow Social Work England standards, and a GP receptionist must follow data protection law.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Both workers are described correctly. But nothing compares how the rules affect them, such as the clear boundaries against the extra recording, or the training needed.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example compare the two roles? What conclusion does it reach?

check.q: Which statement compares the effect of codes of practice in the two settings?
options: Registered social workers follow standards set by Social Work England, which guide their daily work.
Staff in both settings must follow laws and codes, which are important for safe practice overall.
Both must protect information, but social workers have stronger professional standards.
The surgery is a larger organisation than the project, so it has many more rules to follow.
check.why: A comparison needs both settings and a difference between them. The social worker option is the tempting Merit-level answer: it is accurate and specific, but it covers one setting only.

requirements.need: Evaluate the effect on service users in both settings.
requirements.fromSpec: Reach valid conclusions about how legislation and codes affect individuals using the settings.
requirements.means: Say how rights and protections look from a service user's side, including any downsides such as delays.
requirements.example: Data protection law gives young carers confidentiality, which builds trust. Yet it can stop the surgery telling the school about a child's caring role, so the protection may also slow help.
requirements.nearMiss: Data protection law gives young carers confidentiality, which builds trust in both the project and the surgery.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives a correct benefit for service users but no drawback, so the evaluation is one-sided. The same law can slow information sharing with the school.
requirements.explainPrompt: What is the benefit of confidentiality in the example? What is the drawback?

check.q: Which evaluation of data protection law for young carers is balanced?
options: It protects confidentiality, which builds trust and makes young carers more likely to seek help.
It builds trust, but it can stop the surgery telling the school about a child's caring role.
It stops the surgery sharing information with others, which can delay help for a young carer.
It is a law that all staff in both settings must follow when handling any personal data.
check.why: Evaluation weighs benefits against drawbacks for service users. The benefit-only option is tempting because it is accurate and applied, but it gives one side, which is the Merit-level trap.

requirements.need: Reach your own conclusions from your own research into how each organisation puts policy into practice.
requirements.fromSpec: Draw on research to deepen understanding and arrive at original and valid conclusions about implementation.
requirements.means: Use sources about each setting, such as its website or inspection reports. Then add a judgement of your own.
requirements.example: The project's published safeguarding policy matches the Children and Families Act 2014, but its reliance on volunteers suggests that implementation could be uneven. It follows the law yet is vulnerable.
requirements.nearMiss: The project's published safeguarding policy matches the Children and Families Act 2014, and it relies on volunteers to run its clubs.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Both findings are correct, but nothing is concluded from them. It never judges whether relying on volunteers might make delivery uneven.
requirements.explainPrompt: What is the 'original' part of the conclusion?

check.q: Which safeguarding conclusion for Fenhaven is reasoned from your own research?
options: Its published policy matches the Children and Families Act 2014, so it follows the law.
A national charity says that projects like Fenhaven often struggle to deliver policy evenly.
Safeguarding is vital in work with young carers, and Fenhaven clearly treats it seriously.
Its policy matches the Act, but reliance on volunteers suggests delivery could be uneven.
check.why: An original conclusion is reasoned from your own evidence, here by comparing the policy with how it is delivered. Matching the policy to the Act, the tempting option, reports a finding but draws no conclusion about delivery.

requirements.need: Judge whether policy has really improved health and wellbeing. Use evidence.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate whether policy making has improved health and wellbeing of service users.
requirements.means: Look for outcomes, not just intentions: are users better off?
requirements.example: The Children and Families Act 2014 gave young carers a right to assessment, and Fenhaven reports more referrals. But numbers do not show whether wellbeing improved, so the evidence is only partly convincing.
requirements.nearMiss: The Children and Families Act 2014 gave young carers a right to assessment, and Fenhaven reports more referrals.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives real evidence. But it treats more referrals as if they showed better wellbeing. It does not ask whether wellbeing has really changed.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example say it cannot prove? Why is that good evaluation?

check.q: Which is evidence that policy has improved young carers' wellbeing?
options: Fenhaven reports more referrals since the Children and Families Act 2014.
The surgery has set up a young carers register, as the Act expects.
Young carers report feeling less isolated after joining the project.
The project has a published safeguarding policy that follows the law.
check.why: Outcome evidence shows a change in young carers' lives. More referrals, the tempting option, show that the duty is being used, but they do not show that anyone's wellbeing has improved.

requirements.need: Compare the effects in two different settings.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate whether policy making has improved wellbeing in different settings.
requirements.means: Say whether the improvement is similar or different in a charity and a health setting. Say why.
requirements.example: In the surgery the register helps identify adults and children quickly, but the charity can offer breaks, so wellbeing gains look larger in the charity.
requirements.nearMiss: Both the surgery and the charity help young carers, the surgery through its register and the charity through clubs and breaks.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It describes what each setting does, but compares nothing; it never says where wellbeing gains look larger or why.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why might the same policy produce different results in the two settings?

check.q: Which best explains why wellbeing gains differ between the surgery and the charity?
options: Their roles, funding and ability to offer practical support differ.
The charity has fewer service users, so each one receives better care.
Young carers at the surgery are healthier, so they have less need of support.
The surgery is part of the NHS, so it values young carers' wellbeing less.
check.why: Context shapes results: the charity can offer breaks and clubs, but the surgery's role is mainly identification. The 'fewer service users' option is tempting but assumes numbers, not roles and funding, drive the difference.

requirements.need: Consider the role of structures such as Integrated Care Boards in local results.
requirements.fromSpec: Use research to reach valid conclusions on how policy and commissioning affect settings.
requirements.means: Name current bodies correctly. Say how they affect services. Integrated Care Boards replaced Clinical Commissioning Groups in 2022.
requirements.example: Integrated Care Boards decide how NHS money is used locally, so whether Quayside prioritises young carers partly depends on their plans. This links a national policy to a local gap.
requirements.nearMiss: Integrated Care Boards decide how NHS money is used locally, and they replaced Clinical Commissioning Groups. Quayside is commissioned through its Integrated Care Board.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It names the body and its role, correctly. But it does not link the body to the local result. It never explains how the board's plans affect whether Quayside prioritises young carers.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which body does the example name, and what does it control?

check.q: Which body now decides how NHS money is used locally, including for Quayside Surgery?
options: The commissioning body that planned local services before 2022.
The Integrated Care Board, which covers the surgery's local area.
The Department of Health and Social Care, which commissions each practice.
The council's social care committee, which funds GP practices.
check.why: Integrated Care Boards replaced Clinical Commissioning Groups in 2022. The pre-2022 body is tempting because it did the same job, but it no longer exists.

parallelCase.title: Bernard Achterberg in Skerrow Bay
parallelCase.summary:
Setting: Skerrow Bay, a fictional fishing town.
Bernard Achterberg, age 73: He is a retired ferry purser. He lives in sheltered housing with his husband, Teun. They have been together for over 40 years.
His condition: Eighteen months ago he was diagnosed with dementia with Lewy bodies. Some days he is alert and chatty. Other days he is drowsy and confused.
His symptoms: He sometimes sees small animals that are not there. He acts out dreams at night and has a shuffling walk.
What matters to him: He used to fix the boiler for the whole block and still wants to be useful. He loves ferry timetables and likes tea in a particular mug. He dislikes noisy lounges.
His care: Care staff visit twice daily. They ask both men how they want care to be done. A community nurse reviews his medication, because some medicines can make his symptoms worse.
Teun: He is tired and worried about falls. He wants Bernard to keep as much independence as possible.
What is changing: Bernard is becoming more dependent on others.
The task: Show how dementia progressively affects Bernard's whole life. Show how holistic (whole-person), person-centred care and current practice meet his needs.

requirements.need: Judge how the progressive effects of dementia (effects that get worse over time) change every part of health and wellbeing.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate the effects of different types of dementia on all aspects of an individual's life.
requirements.means: Do not stop at today's symptoms. Show how physical, mental, emotional and social life change over time and which changes matter most.
requirements.example: Bernard's fluctuating alertness limits his independence now, but as the condition progresses falls and confusion will probably affect his social life and Teun's health too. The social and emotional decline may therefore be as serious as the physical.
requirements.nearMiss: Bernard has dementia with Lewy bodies, and his alertness fluctuates, he sees small animals that are not there and he has a shuffling walk.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is accurate and applied to Bernard. But it lists current symptoms only. It shows no change over time and no judgement of wider effects on his life or Teun's.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example move from today to later? What does 'as serious as the physical' judge?

check.q: Which sentence judges the progressive effects of dementia on Bernard's wellbeing?
options: Falls and confusion will probably cut his social contact, harming him as much as his movement.
Bernard has hallucinations, drowsy days and a shuffling walk, and these affect his daily life now.
Bernard's dementia will get worse over time, so he will need more care than he does at present.
Bernard's dementia affects his physical, social and emotional health, each in a different way.
check.why: Judging progression means predicting how effects change over time and across areas of life, and which matter most. The tempting symptoms option describes his current condition accurately but shows no change and no wider effect.

requirements.need: Draw together types, causes, symptoms and effects of dementia.
requirements.fromSpec: Draw together knowledge of types, causes, symptoms and effects.
requirements.means: Link what causes Lewy body dementia to the symptoms and then to daily life.
requirements.example: In dementia with Lewy bodies, protein deposits in the brain affect alertness and movement, which explains why Bernard has both confusion and a shuffling walk. This is different from the memory-led picture many people expect.
requirements.nearMiss: Bernard has dementia with Lewy bodies, which causes confusion, hallucinations and a shuffling walk, so he needs help with daily care.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It joins type to symptoms and needs. But it gives no cause of the symptoms. So it never explains why Lewy body dementia affects both thinking and movement.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example connect cause, symptom and effect? Why is that different from a definition?

check.q: Which sentence links the cause of Bernard's dementia to his symptoms?
options: Bernard has dementia with Lewy bodies, which causes hallucinations, confusion and a shuffling walk.
Dementia is simply caused by ageing, so memory loss is the main sign of Bernard's condition.
Protein deposits in his brain affect alertness and movement, so he is confused and shuffles.
Lewy body dementia is the same as Alzheimer's disease, with memory loss always coming first.
check.why: Linking shows how a cause leads to symptoms. The tempting type-and-symptoms option names both but gives no cause, and the other two confuse ageing and Alzheimer's disease with Lewy body dementia.

requirements.need: Give anonymised examples (with no names) of how workers' understanding of progression leads to good practice.
requirements.fromSpec: Give anonymised examples from settings of how workers' understanding of progressive effects leads to good practice.
requirements.means: Use short examples with no names or identifying detail. Show a worker adapting care because they understood the condition.
requirements.example: A care worker who knew that alertness fluctuates scheduled personal care in the late morning when the resident was clearest, which reduced distress. (Anonymised.)
requirements.nearMiss: A care worker who understood dementia adapted her routine to suit the resident, which helped to reduce distress. (Anonymised.)
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is anonymised and links to understanding, but it is vague. It says nothing about the feature of progression, such as fluctuating alertness, that the worker acted on.
requirements.explainPrompt: Why does the example not use a name? What does the worker's knowledge change?

check.q: Which is an anonymised example of good practice based on understanding progression?
options: A care worker timed washing for when Bernard Achterberg was clearest, which reduced his distress.
Care workers are kind to residents with dementia and try hard to make them comfortable.
A care worker timed washing for late morning, because the manager's rota required it that way.
A care worker timed washing for late morning, when a resident was clearest, which cut distress.
check.why: An anonymised example removes identifying detail but still shows practice based on understanding. The named version is tempting because it is specific, but it breaches confidentiality.

requirements.need: Refer accurately to independent research. Use it to justify your conclusions.
requirements.fromSpec: Carry out detailed independent research and analysis, accurately referenced.
requirements.means: Cite recognised sources such as the Alzheimer's Society or NICE (the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence). Use them for reasoning.
requirements.example: Alzheimer's Society guidance explains that some antipsychotic drugs can be harmful in Lewy body dementia. This supports the judgement that medicine reviews are essential in Bernard's care.
requirements.nearMiss: Alzheimer's Society guidance explains that some antipsychotic drugs can be harmful in Lewy body dementia, and Bernard's medicines are reviewed by a community nurse.
requirements.whyNearMiss: The source is named and correct, but it is not used to reach a judgement. So the conclusion that Bernard's medicines need regular review is never drawn.
requirements.explainPrompt: How is the source used in the example?

check.q: Which use of a reference best justifies a conclusion about Bernard's medicines?
options: Alzheimer's Society guidance on harmful antipsychotics supports regular medicine reviews for him.
Alzheimer's Society guidance on dementia is listed in the references at the end of the report.
A website says some drugs may be harmful in dementia, so his medicines should be reviewed.
Alzheimer's Society guidance says that dementia affects memory, thinking and everyday life for people.
check.why: A good reference is named, accurate and used in the argument. Listing it at the end is the tempting option: the source is named, but it supports no conclusion.

requirements.need: Justify the benefits of holistic (whole-person), person-centred care. Cover all of daily living.
requirements.fromSpec: Justify the strengths and advantages of holistic person-centred care; apply to all aspects of daily living.
requirements.means: Show how care covers physical, emotional, social and practical needs and why that gives better outcomes.
requirements.example: Planning care around Bernard's love of fixing things, for example a safe task in the building, supports his identity and mood as well as his activity. A task-only routine would miss this.
requirements.nearMiss: Care staff visit Bernard twice daily to support him with daily living, and a community nurse reviews his medicines. This keeps him safe and well.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It covers physical care and safety, but it is task-based. It does not link care to Bernard's identity or wishes, such as his wish to stay useful.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example connect a hobby to wellbeing?

check.q: Which approach to Bernard's care is holistic and person-centred?
options: Include washing, meals and medicines, each at a set time, twice a day.
Include support for Teun as well as Bernard, but nothing based on his own interests.
Include every health professional who is involved and when each will visit Bernard.
Include a safe repair task and calm spaces, as well as washing and medicines.
check.why: Holistic person-centred care fits the whole person, including identity and interests. The tempting task-based routine covers his physical needs well, but it would miss what makes him who he is.

requirements.need: Explain the consequences of not following a person-centred approach.
requirements.fromSpec: Include the consequences of not following a person-centred approach.
requirements.means: Say what could go wrong: loss of dignity, distress, loss of skills.
requirements.example: If staff rushed Bernard through a noisy lounge routine, he might become agitated and withdraw. His independence could shrink faster than necessary.
requirements.nearMiss: If staff did not follow a person-centred approach, Bernard might be unhappy and his care might be less good.
requirements.whyNearMiss: A consequence is named, but only vaguely. It does not explain how, or what Bernard would lose, such as his independence.
requirements.explainPrompt: What consequences does the example suggest for Bernard?

check.q: Which is a consequence of not following a person-centred approach with Bernard?
options: Staff may finish their routines more quickly, so his care is improved overall.
He may become agitated and withdraw, and his independence may shrink sooner.
His dementia would progress faster because of the way that staff treat him daily.
He would be more settled, because a fixed routine is always more predictable.
check.why: A consequence has to be specific to the person: distress and loss of independence for Bernard. The 'faster progression' option is tempting, but care approaches affect distress and function, not the underlying disease.

requirements.need: Base your evaluation on independent, referenced research into this person's care.
requirements.fromSpec: Carry out independent detailed research into the care for the individual; accurately referenced.
requirements.means: Link published person-centred principles to what Bernard really receives.
requirements.example: Kitwood's person-centred approach stresses personhood. For Bernard, using his preferred mug and calm spaces respects this, which backs the claim that small choices matter.
requirements.nearMiss: Kitwood's person-centred approach stresses personhood, and person-centred care is important for people with dementia such as Bernard.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Kitwood is named and linked to Bernard's dementia, but not to any detail of his care. So the claim that small choices matter is not backed.
requirements.explainPrompt: How does the example tie a theory to Bernard's life?

check.q: Which use of research best backs the claim that small choices matter for Bernard?
options: Kitwood's work on personhood is cited to show that person-centred care matters for everyone.
Kitwood wrote a well-known book on dementia care, which many care workers have read.
Kitwood's work on personhood shows why his preferred mug and calm spaces respect him.
A study shows that people with dementia like familiar objects such as a favourite mug.
check.why: Research justifies a claim when a named source is tied to the individual's details. Citing Kitwood for everyone, the tempting option, is named and accurate but never reaches Bernard's mug or his dislike of noisy lounges.

requirements.need: Evaluate how well current practice manages the effects of dementia for this person.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate how managing and alleviating symptoms meets the needs of the individual.
requirements.means: Judge how far each part of the care meets his needs, and where gaps remain.
requirements.example: Visiting twice daily covers basic care, but Teun's worry about falls suggests night-time risk is not covered. Current practice is good for routine needs but incomplete for safety.
requirements.nearMiss: Care staff visit twice daily and a community nurse reviews Bernard's medication, which meets his routine needs.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It judges the practice, but only its strengths. It never asks whether gaps remain, such as Teun's worry about falls at night.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which gap does the example find?

check.q: Which evaluation of Bernard's current care is complete?
options: Twice-daily visits, a nurse's medicine review and tea in his mug show good practice.
Twice-daily visits are too few, and Teun is tired and worried about falls at night.
Bernard has care staff twice daily, and a community nurse reviews his medicines.
Visits twice daily cover routine needs, but night-time falls risk is uncovered.
check.why: Evaluating practice looks for strengths and gaps against needs. The strengths-only option is the tempting Merit-level answer: it is accurate and applied, but it never asks what the care leaves uncovered.

requirements.need: Use current best practice and professional opinion to justify your judgements.
requirements.fromSpec: Base conclusions on research into current best practice and professional opinion.
requirements.means: Cite current guidance (such as NICE or recognised charities) and professional views. Use them in your argument.
requirements.example: NICE guidance advises regular medication review for people with dementia, and the community nurse's review follows this, so this part of practice is sound.
requirements.nearMiss: The community nurse reviews Bernard's medication, which is good practice for someone with dementia.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It judges the practice sound but cites no guidance, such as NICE, so the judgement rests on assertion.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example compare Bernard's care with?

check.q: What makes a source of best practice suitable for justifying a judgement?
options: It is current, evidence-based guidance, such as NICE guidance.
It reflects what most care staff at Skerrow Bay prefer to do.
It is the lowest-cost approach that the local council could afford.
It is a long-established approach that staff have always used.
check.why: Best practice rests on current evidence. Long-established habit is the tempting option because experience feels reliable, but familiarity is not evidence, and cost and preference do not show what works.

requirements.need: Show how your research deepened your understanding and led to an original conclusion.
requirements.fromSpec: Show how research deepened understanding to arrive at original and valid conclusions, using vocational language.
requirements.means: Say what you learned and how it changed your view, using correct terms.
requirements.example: A first view might be that memory support is the priority, but research shows that fluctuating cognition and movement are key in this type of dementia. Falls prevention then matters more than memory aids.
requirements.nearMiss: Research showed that dementia with Lewy bodies affects alertness and movement as well as memory, which gave a fuller picture of Bernard's needs.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It shows research widening understanding. But no view changes and no priority is concluded, such as falls prevention over memory aids.
requirements.explainPrompt: What changed in the writer's thinking?

check.q: Which statement shows research changing a first view into an original conclusion?
options: Research gave a much clearer picture of the types of dementia and the symptoms of each type.
Memory aids seemed the priority, but research on movement and alertness puts falls first.
Alzheimer's Society guidance confirmed that memory support is the priority for Bernard's care.
Research suggests several priorities, so memory aids and falls prevention should both be covered.
check.why: An original conclusion shows the view changing because of research and reaches a reasoned priority. The tempting 'several priorities' option sounds balanced, but it reaches no conclusion about which matters more.

requirements.need: Link type, symptoms, needs and care provision when justifying judgements.
requirements.fromSpec: Use analysis of type of dementia, symptoms, needs and care provision to justify validity.
requirements.means: Join the four together in one argument.
requirements.example: Because Lewy body dementia affects movement and alertness, Bernard needs falls checks and flexible timing. The care plan should be flexible for these needs, which it currently only partly does.
requirements.nearMiss: Because Lewy body dementia affects movement and alertness, Bernard needs falls checks and flexible timing of care.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It links type, symptoms and needs, but stops before provision; it never judges whether the care plan currently meets those needs.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which four ideas does the example link?

check.q: Which sentence links type, symptoms, needs and care provision for Bernard?
options: Bernard has Lewy body dementia, a shuffling walk, falls checks and a care plan in place.
Bernard's care plan covers his needs, which come from the type of dementia that he has.
Lewy body dementia affects movement, so falls checks are needed, but only partly given.
Bernard's dementia affects movement and alertness, and so he needs regular falls checks.
check.why: Good linking runs from type to needs to provision, and judges the fit. The tempting 'type to needs' option is accurate and applied, but stops before asking whether the care plan provides what he needs.

parallelCase.title: Kacper and Amara at Cedarwood Forest Nursery
parallelCase.summary:
Setting: Cedarwood, a fictional forest nursery. Children spend most of the day outdoors in all weathers.
Kacper, age 3 years 2 months: He uses about ten words in Polish and English together, and mostly points. He follows simple instructions, plays alongside others and loves digging.
Kacper's family: His grandmother brings him to the nursery. She speaks mainly Polish, so staff and the health visitor use an interpreter for important meetings. Kacper did not attend the first health visitor review.
Amara, age 5 years 1 month: She has older siblings. She reads simple books, threads small beads easily and writes her name. She is kind to younger children and loves singing.
Amara's difficulties: She gets upset when games change. She sometimes plays alone. Her family want to work with the nursery.
How staff observe: They use narrative notes, checklists and a time sample.
Who the nursery works with: The setting uses the early years framework, including the progress check at age two. It works with the health visitor and a speech and language therapist.
The task: Decide which theories (such as Piaget, Vygotsky and Bowlby) help explain the children. Decide which assessment methods are reliable. Decide how to act on early signs.

requirements.need: Evaluate how far each selected theory helps explain and support a child's development.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate the extent to which theories can be applied in practice to support children at different stages.
requirements.means: Say how useful each theory is for each child, not just what it says.
requirements.example: Vygotsky's idea of learning with a more knowledgeable other helps explain Kacper's language, since practitioners can model and extend his words. It helps less in explaining why his speech is delayed.
requirements.nearMiss: Vygotsky's idea of a more knowledgeable other helps explain Kacper's language, since practitioners can model and extend his words.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It applies the theory to Kacper correctly, but only in its favour. It never judges a limit, such as the theory not explaining why his speech is delayed.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does the example say Vygotsky explains well, and what not?

check.q: Which statement evaluates Vygotsky's theory for Kacper?
options: Vygotsky's idea of a more knowledgeable other means that adults can model words for Kacper.
Vygotsky's theory is important and is still widely used in early years settings today.
Vygotsky described a zone of proximal development, between what a child can do alone and with help.
It guides how to support Kacper's language, but does not explain why his speech is delayed.
check.why: Evaluation judges how far a theory helps, including what it cannot explain. The tempting option applies the theory to Kacper accurately but only in its favour, so no limit is weighed.

requirements.need: Weigh up the advantages and disadvantages of the theories.
requirements.fromSpec: Consider advantages and disadvantages of selected theories.
requirements.means: Every theory has strengths and limits. Name both.
requirements.example: Piaget's stages help staff expect what Amara can do in play, but they underestimate what children achieve with an adult's support, so a nursery practitioner should not rely on them alone.
requirements.nearMiss: Piaget's stages help staff to expect what Amara can do in play, so the nursery can plan suitable activities for her.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives an advantage applied to Amara, but no disadvantage. So the theory is not weighed.
requirements.explainPrompt: What limit does the example find in Piaget's theory?

check.q: Which evaluation of Piaget's theory for nursery practice is fair?
options: Stages help staff expect what Amara can do, but understate what adult support enables.
Piaget's stages help staff to expect what Amara can do in her play at five.
Piaget's theory is outdated, so it is of no use to staff working with young children today.
Piaget described stages of development, from sensorimotor to formal operational thinking.
check.why: A fair evaluation weighs strengths and weaknesses. The strengths-only option is tempting because it is accurate and applied to Amara, but it gives one side, and the weaknesses-only option is equally one-sided.

requirements.need: Use research to reach reasoned conclusions and recommendations. Keep them short.
requirements.fromSpec: Use detailed analysis and research to reach reasoned and valid conclusions and recommendations, articulated concisely and professionally.
requirements.means: Support your points with recognised sources. Finish with practical recommendations.
requirements.example: Bowlby's attachment work suggests Amara's distress at change may link to security, so predictable routines and warning before changes would fit. Research on attachment backs this approach.
requirements.nearMiss: Amara should be given warning before games change, because she gets upset when routines change and this may help her feel secure.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives a sensible recommendation with a reason from her behaviour. But it names no theory or research to support it.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which part of the example is the recommendation and which is the research?

check.q: Which recommendation for Amara is linked to theory and evidence?
options: Give her warning before changes, because she gets upset when games change.
Give her harder activities, because she reads simple books and threads beads easily.
Give warning before changes, as attachment research links security to routine.
Ask her parents to review routines at home, because attachment difficulties start there.
check.why: A good recommendation is reasoned from theory and research, here Bowlby's attachment work. The tempting observation-only option is sensible and applied, but gives no theory or evidence to support it.

requirements.need: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of each assessment approach.
requirements.fromSpec: Evaluate strengths and weaknesses of each approach in identifying differing needs and atypical development.
requirements.means: Compare approaches such as narrative notes, checklists and time samples for what they can and cannot show.
requirements.example: A checklist quickly shows that Kacper has fewer words than expected, but narrative notes show he communicates by pointing and gesture. The narrative gives richer insight, though it takes longer.
requirements.nearMiss: A checklist shows that Kacper has fewer words than expected, and narrative notes show that he communicates by pointing and gesture.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Each method is applied to Kacper correctly. But the answer does not weigh their strengths and weaknesses, such as speed against richness of detail.
requirements.explainPrompt: What does each method reveal in the example? Which is richer?

check.q: Which statement evaluates assessment methods?
options: A checklist shows that Kacper has fewer words than expected, and a narrative shows he points.
A checklist is quick but narrow, while a narrative shows more detail but takes time.
A time sample records what a child is doing at set intervals during the session.
Checklists, narrative notes and time samples are all used by staff at Cedarwood.
check.why: Evaluation weighs what each method shows against its limits. The tempting option applies both methods to Kacper accurately, but it only reports what each found and never weighs one against the other.

requirements.need: Judge the risks and limitations of methods, such as bias and context.
requirements.fromSpec: Make reasoned judgements about the risks and limitations of the assessment methods used.
requirements.means: Think about observer bias, the setting, the child's mood, and how typical the observation was.
requirements.example: Watching Kacper on a day he was tired may under-represent his language. Repeating the observation on another day would reduce this risk.
requirements.nearMiss: Observing Kacper on a day he was tired might not show his full language, so the observation could have been wrong.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It identifies the limit and gives a reason. But it proposes no way to reduce it, such as repeating the observation on another day.
requirements.explainPrompt: What risk does the example identify? How does it deal with it?

check.q: Staff observed Kacper once, on a day he was tired. Which step best reduces the risk of bias?
options: Make the observation longer on the same day, so that there is more evidence.
Use a checklist, because ticks are objective and not affected by mood.
Compare Kacper with other three-year-olds, to check whether he is typical.
Repeat the observation on other days and at different times of the day.
check.why: Repeating observations in different contexts reduces the effect of one bad day. A longer observation on the same day is tempting because more evidence feels safer, but it keeps the same bias.

requirements.need: Use your own observations to show real insight into stages of development.
requirements.fromSpec: Draw on the observations carried out to show a valid insight into children's stages.
requirements.means: Refer to what you saw and link it to milestones.
requirements.example: Observing Amara thread tiny beads suggests fine motor control above her age expectation, and her upset when games change suggests she may need support with flexibility.
requirements.nearMiss: Amara threads small beads easily and gets upset when games change.
requirements.whyNearMiss: The observations are specific and accurate, but they are not interpreted. It does not link them to expected milestones, or say what they show about her stage of development.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which observed behaviour supports each point?

check.q: What makes an observation valid evidence (true and useful) of Amara's stage of development?
options: It records everything Amara did, in great detail, over the whole morning.
It records what she did and links it to the milestones expected at her age.
It describes how she seemed, such as 'upset' or 'clever', in the observer's words.
It is dated and signed, so that others can see who made it and when.
check.why: Valid observation records evidence and interprets it against milestones. A very detailed record is the tempting option, since detail feels thorough, but without milestones it shows nothing about her stage.

requirements.need: Show how assessment methods help children reach their potential.
requirements.fromSpec: Consider how assessment methods contribute to the process and support children to reach their full potential.
requirements.means: Say what the assessment leads to.
requirements.example: The observations give Kacper's grandmother and therapist a shared picture of his communication, so help can be targeted. Without them, his needs could have stayed hidden.
requirements.nearMiss: Observation of Kacper's communication shows that he uses about ten words and points, which is useful information for staff.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is accurate and useful. But it does not say how the information is used, such as who it informs or how help is targeted.
requirements.explainPrompt: Who uses the information in the example?

check.q: What is the main purpose of assessing Kacper's communication?
options: To compare Kacper with other children and see where he ranks.
To record what staff have done, as evidence for inspectors.
To plan help that is targeted to what Kacper needs most now.
To label Kacper's difficulty early so that everyone recognises it.
check.why: Assessment informs support. Comparing Kacper with other children is the tempting option, as milestones involve comparison, but ranking him is not the purpose, and labelling does not help him.

requirements.need: Judge how theory and assessment together help staff spot early that development is delayed or advanced.
requirements.fromSpec: Make reasoned judgements about how theories and assessment enable early recognition.
requirements.means: Show how a theory tells you what to expect and assessment shows what is happening.
requirements.example: Developmental milestones tell staff that Kacper's ten words at 3 years 2 months are fewer than expected. The observations confirm the gap, so the theory and assessment together flag the concern.
requirements.nearMiss: Developmental theory gives staff a picture of how children usually develop, and the observations record what Kacper can do.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Both theory and observation are mentioned, but they are not combined. It never says that the milestones show ten words are fewer than expected.
requirements.explainPrompt: How do the two work together in the example?

check.q: What does theory add to an assessment of Kacper?
options: It gives a benchmark of what is typically expected at his age.
It replaces observation with predictions of what a child can do.
It explains the cause of any delay that observations show.
It lets staff compare Kacper with older children to see how far behind.
check.why: Theory gives a benchmark against which observations are interpreted. The 'cause of delay' option is tempting because Kacper's speech is delayed, but theories of development do not by themselves explain why a particular child is delayed.

requirements.need: Explain why early recognition (spotting needs early) is important.
requirements.fromSpec: Consider the importance of early recognition.
requirements.means: Say what changes if help starts earlier.
requirements.example: Early help for Kacper's language can prevent frustration and help him prepare for school. Later help often costs more effort.
requirements.nearMiss: Early recognition is important because Kacper's language needs support, and problems could get worse if help is delayed.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It gives a reason, but a general one. It names no specific consequence for Kacper, such as frustration or readiness for school.
requirements.explainPrompt: Which consequence of early help does the example give?

check.q: Which is a reason that early recognition matters for Kacper?
options: It means the nursery will have fewer children needing extra support in later years.
It shows the setting is meeting the requirements of its next inspection visit.
Difficulties can be tackled before they build up and affect his school readiness.
It proves that Kacper has a language disorder, so a diagnosis can be recorded.
check.why: Early recognition matters because it prevents difficulties building up for the child. The diagnosis option is tempting, but recognising a concern early is not the same as proving a disorder.

requirements.need: Suggest interventions (actions) and support that follow from assessment.
requirements.fromSpec: Suggest forms of intervention and support that can be put in place as a result of assessment.
requirements.means: Name realistic steps and who does them.
requirements.example: A referral to the speech and language therapist and daily small-group story time would support Kacper. For Amara, extension activities and a visual timetable would challenge and reassure her.
requirements.nearMiss: Kacper should be referred to the speech and language therapist, and Amara should be given some extra activities.
requirements.whyNearMiss: Kacper's action is specific, but Amara's is vague. So the answer does not follow from assessment with a clear action for both children.
requirements.explainPrompt: Who does what in the example?

check.q: Which is a specific intervention for Kacper?
options: Refer Kacper to the speech and language therapist and begin small-group story time.
Give Kacper extra support with his talking, as soon as his needs have been agreed.
Spend more time with Kacper during the day, to help his language to develop further.
Ask Kacper's grandmother to keep supporting him in whichever way she thinks best.
check.why: A specific intervention names an action and who will carry it out. The other options are tempting because they sound caring, but each leaves out who does what.

requirements.need: Reach a justified conclusion on the positive impact for outcomes.
requirements.fromSpec: Arrive at a justified conclusion of how this can have a positive impact on outcomes.
requirements.means: Finish by judging the likely effect, with caution.
requirements.example: Targeted support will probably improve Kacper's communication and confidence, although progress will vary. Amara's needs are met by routine and challenge, which supports both her achievement and her security.
requirements.nearMiss: Targeted support will improve Kacper's communication and confidence, and Amara's needs are met by routine and challenge.
requirements.whyNearMiss: It is a positive conclusion linked to both children. But it sounds certain and does not admit that progress will vary.
requirements.explainPrompt: What caution does the example include?

check.q: Which conclusion about the impact of support on outcomes is justified?
options: Targeted support will improve Kacper's communication, and he will catch up by school.
Targeted support will probably improve Kacper's talking, though progress will vary.
Support will be good for both children, because early help is always positive.
Kacper's progress cannot be predicted, so no conclusion about support can be reached.
check.why: A justified conclusion uses evidence and admits uncertainty. The tempting 'will catch up' option is confident and positive, but a certain prediction is not justified when progress varies.
